DysonNet: Constant-Time Local Updates for Neural Quantum States

Lucas Winter Affiliation: Faculty of Physics, University of Vienna, Boltzmanngasse 5, 1090 Vienna, Austria    Andreas Nunnenkamp Affiliation: Faculty of Physics, University of Vienna, Boltzmanngasse 5, 1090 Vienna, Austria
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Neural quantum states (NQS) provide a flexible variational framework for many-body wavefunctions, but suffer from high computational cost and limited interpretability. We introduce DysonNet, a broad class of NQS that couples strictly local nonlinearities through global linear layers. This structure is analogous to a truncated Dyson series which gives an intuitive interpretation of local wavefunction updates as scattering from static impurities. By resumming the scattering series, single-spin-flip updates can be computed in 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) time, independent of system size, using an algorithm we call ABACUS. Implementing DysonNet with the state-space model S4, we obtain up to 230×230\times speedups over Vision-Transformers for computing the local estimator. This corresponds to an asymptotic 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) improvement in training-time scaling, reaching 𝒪⁡(N​log2​N)\mathcal{O}(N\log^{2}N) total training complexity in area-law phases. Benchmarks on the 1D long-range Ising model and frustrated J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} chains show that DysonNet matches state-of-the-art NQS accuracy while removing the dominant local-update overhead. More broadly, our results suggest a route to scalable NQS architectures where physical interpretability directly enables computational efficiency.

I Introduction

Neural quantum states (NQS) have emerged as a flexible and potentially scalable class of variational wave-function ansätze [7, 39]. Recently, neural quantum states have achieved state-of-the-art accuracy across a wide domain of challenging ground state problems like frustrated magnets [83, 79, 8], the Hubbard model [63, 25, 33], long-ranged quantum systems [61, 74], and fractional quantum Hall problems [22, 21]. Many architectures have been proposed including restricted Boltzmann machines (RBM) [7, 48], convolutional networks (CNN) [44, 19, 42], recurrent networks (RNN) [30, 15], and Transformers (ViT) [69, 79, 61, 72, 9]. One of the main promises of NQS is that their nonlinear structure gives them higher expressive power than conventional Ansätze such as tensor network states (TNS) [85, 14, 55].

The downside of this nonlinear structure is that to update the state after a single spin flip forces a full evaluation of the network. For restricted Boltzmann machines (RBM), local update schemes exist, but their costs scale with system size [7, 50, 54, 10, 20]. Autoregressive (AR) factorization of the wavefunction can make sampling more efficient, but it leaves local update costs unchanged [69, 30]. There are specialized Ansätze like finite receptive field CNNs or local graph neural networks that can trivially be updated in 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) but this is achieved by neglecting any long-range correlations. To our knowledge, no current method endows deep NQS with constant time local updates while retaining their broad expressivity.

This paper closes that gap. We present a constant-time local-update algorithm ABACUS for neural network architectures with linear token mixer and strictly local nonlinearity. The algorithm applies to many popular architectures such as convolutional neural networks [40], linearized attention [61, 60], Fourier layers [43, 68], state space models [24, 23] or graph neural networks [64, 36]. We prove that the change in the network output after a single spin flip can be computed in time independent of NN using precontracted link tensors. We apply the algorithm to DysonNet, a broad class of convolutional NQS. Each layer applies a convolution operator and then a local nonlinearity. DysonNet admits a particularly simple physical interpretation — it is functionally analogous to a truncated Dyson series. Within DysonNet, local updates can be interpreted as scattering at static impurities giving ABACUS a physically intuitive interpretation as resumming the scattering series. Furthermore, DysonNet allows for efficient calculation of the link tensors via convolutions.

We implement DysonNet using the state space model (SSM) S4 [24] as a mixer which is particularly interpretable in terms of a physical Green’s function. We benchmark our model on long-range spin chains, such as the long-range transverse field Ising model (TFIM). This yields up to two orders of magnitude wall-clock speedups over Vision-Transformers [61] at N=1000N=1000 at matched accuracy. We formalize the model class, give the algorithm and proof, describe an efficient implementation, and benchmark accuracy, runtime, and validate scaling to large system sizes. Our work introduces the widely-applicable algorithm ABACUS and the physically interpretable architecture DysonNet that can significantly reduce the computational cost of NQS simulations.

II DysonNet: Physically motivated neural network architecture

A key feature of many quantum many-body ground states is a natural separation of scales: long-wavelength behavior is often universal and can be described by a few collective modes, the basis for effective field theories and the renormalization group. In contrast, short-range physics can be highly complex and non-universal, depending sensitively on microscopic details of the Hamiltonian.

We will start by introducing DysonNet, a class of NQS Ansätze that explicitly builds the separation of correlation scales into their architecture. Each block factorizes the representation into (i) a linear, translation-invariant propagator GG that captures long-wavelength response and (ii) a local nonlinearity D⁡(𝝈)D(\bm{\sigma}) that captures short-range structure. Stacking such blocks yields a representation that is both efficient and interpretable, rather than asking a generic ansatz to discover this structure from scratch.

Definition (DysonNet block).

Let 𝛔∈{±1}N\bm{\sigma}\in\{\pm 1\}^{N} be a spin configuration, 𝐡(l)∈ℝN×d\bm{h}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} a sequence of latent vectors with dd-channels and fix a half–window w∈ℕw\in\mathbb{N}. A single DysonNet block is the map

𝒉(l+1)=D(l)​(𝝈)​G(l)​𝒉(l).\;\bm{h}^{(l+1)}\;=\;D^{(l)}(\bm{\sigma})\;G^{(l)}\,\bm{h}^{(l)}\;.\; (1)

It consists of

(1) Green’s function convolution, GG is a linear, translation–invariant operator along the chain that acts independently on each channel (i.e. it is diagonal in the channel index cc). In real space it acts as a lattice Green’s–function convolution,

(G(l)𝒉)j=∑r∈ℤgr,c(l)hj−r,c,c=1,…,d.\displaystyle(G^{(l)}\bm{h})_{j}\;=\;\sum_{r\in\mathbb{Z}}g_{r,c}^{(l)}\;h_{j-r,c}\,,\quad c=1,\dots,d. (2)

(2) Local nonlinearity D⁡(𝛔)D(\bm{\sigma}) is an input-conditioned matrix multiplication that acts position-wise on each embedding vector in the sequence

(D(l)(𝝈)𝒉)j,c=D(l)(σj−w:j+w)𝒉j.\displaystyle(D^{(l)}(\bm{\sigma})\bm{h})_{j,c}\;=\;D^{(l)}(\sigma_{j-w:j+w})\;\bm{h}_{j}. (3)

The receptive field of the local non-linearity is W=2​w+1W=2w+1 where ww is the half-width.

Stacks are obtained by recursive application of (1).

Here, GG denotes any translationally invariant kernel convolution, such as Fourier layers [43, 68], linearized (Toeplitz) attention [61], state space models [24, 23], or analytical Green’s functions. While limited by finite receptive fields, standard CNN kernels also apply [40]. Depending on the padding scheme, the convolution can support either open or periodic boundary conditions.

The network is composed of a stack of DysonNet blocks followed by a pooling operation, (multiple) densely connected layers, and a nonlinearity. This means the network output is

Ψ⁡(𝝈)=f⁡[A​PM​(Gf​∑M=0L∏l=1MD(l)​(𝝈)​G(l))​E​𝝈],\displaystyle\Psi(\bm{\sigma})=f\bigg[AP_{M}\bigg(G^{f}\sum_{M=0}^{L}\prod_{l=1}^{M}D^{(l)}(\bm{\sigma})G^{(l)}\bigg)E\bm{\sigma}\bigg], (4)

where E∈ℝd×1E\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times 1} is the per-site embedding layer (applied independently at each position), (PM​𝒉)c=1N​∑jhj,c(P_{M}\bm{h})_{c}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j}h_{j,c} is a mean pooling operation. The sum adds a residual connection from the latent activations of each layer to the output. GfG^{f} is the final Green’s function convolution. ff is the final nonlinearity often chosen to be f⁡(x)=log⁡cosh⁡(x)f(x)=\log\cosh(x). AA is the final matrix multiplication chosen to be real valued A∈ℝd×doutA\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{\mathrm{out}}} for stoquastic Hamiltonians or A∈ℂd×doutA\in\mathbb{C}^{d\times d_{\mathrm{out}}} for complex wavefunctions.

While the network definition (4) seems quite complicated at first glance it admits a very simple interpretation. For simplicity, let us assume weight sharing between the different layers G(l)=Gf:=G0G^{(l)}=G_{f}:=G_{0} and D(l)​(𝝈)=D​(𝝈)D^{(l)}(\bm{\sigma})=D(\bm{\sigma}) [86]. We can then interpret the product of layers in Eq. (4) (expression inside round bracket) as an effective propagator GG. Expanding this term yields

G=G0​∑M=0L∏l=1MD⁡(𝝈)​G0=G0+G0​D​(𝝈)​G0+G0​D​(𝝈)​G0​D​(𝝈)​G0+….\displaystyle\begin{split}G&=G_{0}\sum_{M=0}^{L}\prod_{l=1}^{M}D(\bm{\sigma})G_{0}\\ &=G_{0}+G_{0}D(\bm{\sigma})G_{0}+G_{0}D(\bm{\sigma})G_{0}D(\bm{\sigma})G_{0}+\dots.\end{split} (5)

We see the network can be interpreted as a truncated Dyson series. Specifically, we can identify G0G_{0} with the free propagator, and D⁡(𝝈)D(\bm{\sigma}) with the coupling vertex. This further justifies our decision to restrict D⁡(𝝈)D(\bm{\sigma}) to be local. While this correspondence allows one to initialize the network using analytic theory, we learn the weight matrices via gradient descent.

The functional equivalence of the network to a Dyson series clarifies how its parameters control the correlations it can express. With LL layers, the network can represent any non-local power-law or exponentially decaying interaction up to coupling order LL; long-ranged correlations are therefore truncated in coupling order (see appendix A). We stress that by parameterizing GG as a power law, the network can naturally express correlations at criticality making it more expressive than a fixed bond dimension matrix product state. By contrast, the local nonlinearity can, in principle, generate correlations of arbitrarily high coupling order, but only within a finite width WW. Varying the number of layers LL and the nonlinear receptive field WW thus provides a systematic way to improve the expressivity of the model. Nevertheless, there exist ground states with genuinely non-local correlations of arbitrary coupling range, such as phases with intrinsic topological order characterized by non-local Wilson loop operators in 2D [11, 82, 41], for which these truncations are insufficient. Representing such exotic quantum states requires additional techniques.

Model training is performed via Variational Monte-Carlo and Stochastic Reconfiguration [7]. We minimize the variational energy by sampling configurations 𝝈\bm{\sigma} and computing the local energy

Eloc​(𝝈)=∑𝝈′⟨𝝈|H|𝝈′⟩​Ψ⁡(𝝈′)Ψ⁡(𝝈).E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\bm{\sigma})=\sum_{\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}}\langle\bm{\sigma}|H|\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}\rangle\frac{\Psi(\bm{\sigma}^{\prime})}{\Psi(\bm{\sigma})}. (6)

Since both the Metropolis sampling and the local energy calculation involve configurations 𝝈′\bm{\sigma}^{\prime} that differ from 𝝈\bm{\sigma} by only a single spin flip, recomputing the full wavefunction is inefficient. In the next section, we derive an optimized update algorithm to handle these local changes exploiting that the network is equivalent to a Dyson series.

III ABACUS: Asymptotically optimal local updates

We will now derive the update algorithm for the amplitude Ψ⁡(𝝈)\Psi(\bm{\sigma}) after a single spin flip at position jj relative to Ψ⁡(𝝈0)\Psi(\bm{\sigma}_{0}). Importantly, the results of this section apply to any network with linear token mixers M(l)M^{(l)}, not only convolutional token mixers such as in DysonNet. For the DysonNet specialization, we identify M(l)=G(l)M^{(l)}=G^{(l)} and Mf=GfM^{f}=G^{f}. As the local vertex D⁡(𝝈)D(\bm{\sigma}) only changes in a narrow slice of width W=2​w+1W=2w+1 around the flip jj (with half-width ww; see Fig. 1a), we can interpret the update as a scattering process off a localized impurity (the perturbation). This perspective allows us to derive an efficient update algorithm by exactly resumming the Dyson series defined by the network.

We formalize this by decomposing every layer’s nonlinearity D(l)​(𝝈)D^{(l)}(\bm{\sigma}) into a static background D0(l):=D(l)​(𝝈0)D_{0}^{(l)}:=D^{(l)}(\bm{\sigma}_{0}) and a localized perturbation, Δ​D(l)=D(l)​(𝝈)−D(l)​(𝝈0)\Delta D^{(l)}=D^{(l)}(\bm{\sigma})-D^{(l)}(\bm{\sigma}_{0}) that is non-zero only on a narrow slice around jj. Substituting this decomposition into Eq. (4) yields

𝛀⁡(𝝈)=A​PM​(Mf​∑M=0L∏l=1M(D0(l)+Δ​D(l))​M(l))​E​𝝈,\bm{\Omega}(\bm{\sigma})=AP_{M}\!\left(M^{f}\sum_{M=0}^{L}\prod_{l=1}^{M}(D^{(l)}_{0}+\Delta D^{(l)})\,M^{(l)}\right)E\bm{\sigma}, (7)

where 𝛀⁡(𝝈)\bm{\Omega}(\bm{\sigma}) is the activation before the final nonlinearity Ψ⁡(𝝈)=f⁡(𝛀⁡(𝝈))\Psi(\bm{\sigma})=f(\bm{\Omega}(\bm{\sigma})). Intuitively, D0D_{0} acts as the background medium and Δ​D\Delta D as a local scatterer; M(l)M^{(l)} is the propagator spreading the local perturbations and the projector PMP_{M} performs the measurement.

We now need to resum the product in (7). If we naively expand the ordered product in Eq. (7) we formally obtain exponentially many matrix words 𝒪⁡(2L)\mathcal{O}(2^{L}) in the network depth LL. This would be prohibitive for deeper networks. To circumvent this we propose ABACUS (Algorithm II) for computing matrix-vector products like (7) in quadratic time 𝒪⁡(L2)\mathcal{O}(L^{2}) in network depth. The algorithm works by (i) pre-contracting all background propagators D0(⋅)​M(⋅)D_{0}^{(\cdot)}M^{(\cdot)} into environment (link) tensors, and (ii) dynamically resumming the matrix words with a slice-local recurrence.

The link tensors defined for a spin configuration 𝝈0\bm{\sigma}_{0} propagate activations through the frozen background

T(l)\displaystyle T^{(l)} =PM​Mf​(∑M=lL∏n=l+1MD0(n)​M(n))​PS,j⊤,\displaystyle=P_{M}M^{f}\left(\sum_{M=l}^{L}\ \prod_{n=l+1}^{M}D_{0}^{(n)}M^{(n)}\right)P_{S,j}^{\top}, (8)
L(l,m)\displaystyle L^{(l,m)} =PS,j​M(l)​(∏n=m+1l−1D0(n)​M(n))​PS,j⊤,,\displaystyle=P_{S,j}M^{(l)}\left(\prod_{n=m+1}^{l-1}D_{0}^{(n)}M^{(n)}\right)P_{S,j}^{\top},\ , (9)

with 1≤m≤l−21\leq m\leq l-2. Note, the projector PS,jP_{S,j} restricts the activation on a narrow slice [j−w,…​j+w][j-w,\dots j+w] around the update jj. The link tensor T(l):ℝW×d→ℝdT^{(l)}:\mathbb{R}^{W\times d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} (8) lifts slice-restricted activations back to full size and propagates them to the output. L(l,m):ℝW×d→ℝW×dL^{(l,m)}:\mathbb{R}^{W\times d}\to\mathbb{R}^{W\times d} (9) propagates slice-restricted activations through the background between layers mm and ll. Crucially, the link tensors require only linear memory in NN. For the special case of DysonNet they can be constructed in log-linear time 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(N\log N) (see appendix G) for both periodic or open boundary conditions. Physically, the link tensors represent fully dressed Green’s function propagators relative to some background.

Using the link tensors (8) and (9), an update to the wave function amplitude 𝛀⁡(𝝈)\bm{\Omega}(\bm{\sigma}) can be computed by summing the scattering events. Let us define the slice-restricted activations 𝒉~(l)=PS,j​𝒉(l)∈ℝW×d\bm{\tilde{h}}^{(l)}=P_{S,j}\bm{h}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{W\times d} and 𝒉~0(l)=PS,j​𝒉0(l)∈ℝW×d\bm{\tilde{h}}_{0}^{(l)}=P_{S,j}\bm{h}_{0}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{W\times d}. Furthermore, we define the slice-restricted convolution M~(l)=PS,j​M(l)​PS,j⊤∈ℝW×W\tilde{M}^{(l)}=P_{S,j}M^{(l)}P_{S,j}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{W\times W}. The slice-restricted activations can be computed using the following recurrence relation

𝒉~(l)\displaystyle\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(l)} =Δ​D(l)​(𝒉~0(l)+M~(l)​𝒉~(l−1)+∑m=1l−2L(l,m)​𝒉~(m)),\displaystyle=\Delta D^{(l)}\left(\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(l)}_{0}+\tilde{M}^{(l)}\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(l-1)}+\sum_{m=1}^{l-2}L^{(l,m)}\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(m)}\right), (10)
𝛀\displaystyle\bm{\Omega} =A⁡(PM​𝒉~(L)+∑l=1LT(l)​𝒉~(l)).\displaystyle=A\!\left(P_{M}\,\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(L)}+\sum_{l=1}^{L}T^{(l)}\,\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(l)}\right). (11)

This recurrence defines the ABACUS algorithm. Physically, 𝒉~(l)\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(l)} represents the sum of all paths scattered at layer ll. This amplitude sums three components: the unscattered incident wave 𝒉~0(l)\bm{\tilde{h}}_{0}^{(l)}; all paths 𝒉~(l−1)\bm{\tilde{h}}^{(l-1)} scattered at the previous layer l−1l-1; and the cumulative contributions from all prior defects mm, propagated through the background.

In the appendix B we prove the following statement

Theorem I (ABACUS exactness and complexity).

Given a linear token mixer M(l)M^{(l)} and a local non-linearity D(l)​(𝛔)D^{(l)}(\bm{\sigma}), the recurrence (10)–(11) evaluates 𝛀⁡(𝛔)\bm{\Omega}(\bm{\sigma}) exactly for any local update 𝛔=𝛔0+Δ​𝛔\bm{\sigma}=\bm{\sigma}_{0}+\Delta\bm{\sigma}. Given precomputed links of Eq. (8) and (9), the runtime 𝒪⁡(L2​W2​d2)\mathcal{O}(L^{2}W^{2}d^{2}) is constant in NN and the memory 𝒪⁡(N​L2​W​d2)\mathcal{O}(NL^{2}Wd^{2}) is linear in NN.

We note ABACUS applies to any network architecture with a linear token mixer and local nonlinearity, including linearized self-attention and graph neural networks, and is not limited to convolutions. In Appendix I we describe ABACUS in 2D beyond the case considered here. The runtime complexity remains unchanged and depends on the number of tokens WW conditioning the nonlinearity. Note, however, that the structure of MM dictates the link-tensor precomputation cost (Eqs. (8) and (9)): while 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(N\log N) for the DysonNet class M(l)=G(l)M^{(l)}=G^{(l)}, it can increase to 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) for dense, unstructured mixers. We discuss this in detail in the runtime section.

The constant-time complexity O⁡(1)O(1) in Theorem I strictly holds when the hyperparameters ww and LL are independent of system size NN. Physically, this assumption relies on a separation of scales: complex, non-universal correlations are confined to a short range ww, while long-wavelength behaviors are captured by the propagator M(l)M^{(l)} (G(l)G^{(l)}).

A common intuition from perturbation theory is that reproducing algebraic decay (criticality) from a short-range bare propagator requires resumming an infinite Dyson series (L→∞L\to\infty). However, in DysonNet, the propagators G(l)G^{(l)} are learnable, translation-invariant kernels capable of representing power-law decays directly. Consequently, G(l)G^{(l)} should be interpreted not as a bare propagator, but as an effective dressed propagator. We empirically observe that even at criticality, small LL is sufficient to preserve the O⁡(1)O(1) update cost.

The algorithm extends naturally to spin clusters of size nn by increasing the effective slice width to wcluster=w+⌈n/2⌉w_{\mathrm{cluster}}=w+\lceil n/2\rceil. Regarding complexity, while the update step is size-independent, the initial link-tensor construction incurs a quasi-linear 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(N\log N) cost. For estimators requiring 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) evaluations, this overhead amortizes to 𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(\log N) per sample. In the next section, we outline a strategy to amortize the link tensor costs for the sampler.

We propose a Metropolis sampler that addresses two bottlenecks: standard Metropolis updates are inherently sequential and thus underuse GPUs, and our link-tensor construction must be amortized to achieve sublinear cost in system size. The key idea is to treat a batch of spatially separated spin flips as a dilute gas of defects. When the defects are well separated, their scattering signatures do not interfere. We can then evaluate the flips as independent proposals in parallel and reuse the same background link tensors across the batch solving both problems. This approximation introduces a small error in the acceptance ratio, but a screened acceptance rule restores exact detailed balance [67].

Proposals are single-site flips, with occasional global spin inversions to aid mixing. A proposal 𝝈0→𝝈\bm{\sigma}_{0}\to\bm{\sigma} is accepted with Pacc=min⁡{1,R}P_{\rm acc}=\min\{1,R\}, where R=|Ψ⁡(𝝈)|2/|Ψ⁡(𝝈0)|2R=|\Psi(\bm{\sigma})|^{2}/|\Psi(\bm{\sigma}_{0})|^{2}. To amortize the 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(N\log N) cost of constructing the background link tensors, we evaluate a batch of FF single-site proposals in parallel using the static background of the reference 𝝈0\bm{\sigma}_{0}. This relies on the Independent Scattering Approximation: we assume the defects interact with the background but not with each other. Note we are using the term in analogy to scattering theory in disordered media [51, 49], although here the defects are not physical. Detailed sampler settings are listed in Appendix Sec. N. The error induced by neglecting the interaction (multiple scattering) between simultaneous flips is

ϵ⁡(𝝈):=|ΨISA​(𝝈)−Ψ​(𝝈)Ψ⁡(𝝈0)|.\displaystyle\epsilon(\bm{\sigma}):=\left|\frac{\Psi_{\mathrm{ISA}}(\bm{\sigma})-\Psi(\bm{\sigma})}{\Psi(\bm{\sigma}_{0})}\right|. (12)

This error is controlled by the decay of the Green’s function, see appendix D. By enforcing a minimum separation ss between defects, we ensure the propagator connecting any two flips is negligible.

To enforce a minimum spacing between flips, we use a typewriter schedule [4, 27] (see algorithm IV). We partition the lattice into blocks of width s≥ws\geq w. We sweep first over even blocks, then odd blocks. In each active block, we select one site uniformly. This creates a superlattice of defects separated by the spacing ss. We build the link tensors once per sweep (costing 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(N\log N)) and reuse them for all proposals in the batch. Because the proposals are spatially separated, the independent scattering approximation is highly accurate and the error ϵ\bm{\epsilon} can be bounded (see appendix D).

Because ϵ\epsilon is bounded, the Metropolis acceptance rule can be enforced exactly even though the wave-function amplitude is approximate. We recover exact detailed balance using a screened acceptance rule [67]. We accept a proposal based on the approximate ratio R~=|ΨISA​(𝝈)|2/|Ψ⁡(𝝈0)|2\tilde{R}=|\Psi_{\mathrm{ISA}}(\bm{\sigma})|^{2}/|\Psi(\bm{\sigma}_{0})|^{2} and error bound ϵ\epsilon. For a random number u∼𝒰⁡[0,1]u\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1]

  1. 1.

    Fast Accept: If u<R~−ϵu<\tilde{R}-\epsilon, accept immediately.

  2. 2.

    Fast Reject: If u>R~+ϵu>\tilde{R}+\epsilon, reject immediately.

  3. 3.

    Correction: Only in the rare window u∈[R~−ϵ,R~+ϵ]u\in[\tilde{R}-\epsilon,\tilde{R}+\epsilon] do we evaluate the exact interference terms (recomputing the full amplitude).

This scheme allows parallel evaluation without statistical bias; proof see appendix C.

The efficiency depends on the physical correlation length of the system. The decay of correlations determines the required spacing ss to keep ϵ\epsilon small. In appendix E, we derive the amortized per proposal cost

𝒯⁡(N)={𝒪⁡(log2⁡N)Area-law (Gapped),𝒪⁡(Nγ​log⁡N)Power-law (Critical),𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)All-to-all..\displaystyle\mathcal{T}(N)=\begin{cases}\mathcal{O}(\log^{2}N)&\text{Area-law (Gapped)},\\ \mathcal{O}(N^{\gamma}\log N)&\text{Power-law (Critical)},\\ \mathcal{O}(N\log N)&\text{All-to-all}.\end{cases}. (13)

For gapped phases (area-law), the Green’s function decays exponentially, allowing dense packing of updates and polylogarithmic runtime. For critical systems (power-law), the spacing ss must grow with system size, leading to sublinear scaling NγN^{\gamma} (where γ<1\gamma<1 depends on the critical exponent α\alpha). Only in the all-to-all limit does the speedup vanish. In our numerics, we find the empirical error ϵ⁡(𝝈,𝝈0)\epsilon(\bm{\sigma},\bm{\sigma}_{0}) to be small up to very large system sizes N≤1000N\leq 1000 and even on criticality. For practical system sizes, adjusting the spacing ss is unnecessary. This means the method yields a speedups of 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) significantly exceeding the worst case analytical estimates (see appendix F). Another significant practical advantage is that the screened acceptance rule enables reduced precision sampling. While neural quantum states typically require high floating-point precision, this rule permits lower-precision formats, which can yield additional constant speedups of 2×2\times to 4×4\times.

Table 1 contrasts the runtime complexity of DysonNet against standard NQS architectures. Among deep networks, our approach uniquely enables constant-time, 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) spin-flip updates given cached environment (link) tensors. In comparison, Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBM) scale linearly as 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N). Autoregressive (AR) models also face costs of 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) per local update. While AR models can be sampled efficiently, the flip costs induce 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) work for local observables which is their most significant bottleneck. While matrix product states (MPS) and local CNNs also achieve 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) updates, they occupy a restricted expressivity class and fail to efficiently represent long-range power-law correlations.

The fact that local updates can be evaluated in constant time gives a distinctive advantage to DysonNet +ABACUS when evaluating the Hamiltonian (6). Local Hamiltonians generally have 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) connected matrix elements, requiring an equivalent number of network evaluations. RBMs, RNNs and PixelCNNs face a cost of 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) for local updates resulting in a cost of 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) in total. The vision transformer (ViT) network evaluation scales as 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) leading to a cubic cost 𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}). DysonNet improves on all prior approaches by constructing link tensors in 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(N\log N) and using the ABACUS algorithm for updates in 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) given cached link tensors, achieving a log-linear cost 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(N\log N).

Metropolis-Hastings approaches generally suffer from sampling costs of 𝒪⁡(N​τ​Cnetwork)\mathcal{O}(N\tau C_{\text{network}}), leading to scaling of 𝒪⁡(N3​τ)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}\tau) for ViTs and 𝒪⁡(N2​τ)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}\tau) for RBMs. DysonNet+ABACUS improves upon these by ensuring the per-sweep cost is strictly sub-quadratic, 𝒪⁡(𝒯⁡(N)​N​τ)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{T}(N)N\tau), and even log-linear, 𝒪⁡(N​log2​N)\mathcal{O}(N\log^{2}N), in area-law phases. Autoregressive architectures, however, retain the fastest asymptotic sampling capability with a cost of 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N).

When considering total training time, Metropolis approaches remain dominated by the sampling cost, meaning our algorithmic improvements yield asymptotic speedups independent of ground state correlations. Autoregressive models, by contrast, are computationally dominated by the 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) overhead required to evaluate the local Hamiltonian. As a result, in area-law phases where τ∝𝒪⁡(1)\tau\propto\mathcal{O}(1), DysonNet+ABACUS achieves a total training complexity of 𝒪⁡(N​log2​N)\mathcal{O}(N\log^{2}N), which is lower than that of autoregressive approaches. Nevertheless, for systems with divergent autocorrelation time autoregressive approaches remain asymptotically faster. While slower, using Markov chain sampling has the advantage of efficient enforcement of wavefunction symmetries that are difficult to implement in autoregressive architectures.

We noted in the algorithm section that ABACUS applies to any NQS with global linear layers. For dense, unstructured linear mixers, a forward pass typically costs 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}), and constructing/caching the link tensors has the same scaling, 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}), rather than 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(N\log N) for DysonNet. In this regime, ABACUS reduces the cost of a Metropolis sweep of local estimators (i.e., NN single-site proposals) from 𝒪⁡(N​Cfwd)=𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}(NC_{\mathrm{fwd}})=\mathcal{O}(N^{3}) to 𝒪⁡(Cfwd+N)=𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(C_{\mathrm{fwd}}+N)=\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) (for fixed depth and locality window). The corresponding sampling speedups depend on the applicability of the independent-scattering approximation; in this work we only provide rigorous bounds for DysonNet, and we leave a systematic study of sampling speedups for dense mixers to future work.

Finally, we compare asymptotic peak memory usage. For standard autoregressive and Markov chain Monte Carlo architectures, the local estimator introduces a significant bottleneck; evaluating the wavefunction on 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) connected configurations typically incurs an 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) memory cost. DysonNet avoids this quadratic scaling. Because local updates require only slice-local activations and the link tensors scale linearly, the total memory footprint is reduced to 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N). This scaling behavior allows for the simulation of large systems on commodity GPUs that lack the high memory capacity of data-center hardware.

Beyond large system asymptotics, network hyperparameters determine when ABACUS outperforms DysonNet. We illustrate this using the local estimator. With 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) forward passes, the cost of computing the local estimator under DysonNet is 𝒪⁡(N​L​(d​N​log⁡N+d2​N))\mathcal{O}(NL(dN\log N+d^{2}N)). For ABACUS, the dominant cost is computing the (L−1)2(L-1)^{2} interlayer link tensor, which scales as 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N​d2​W)\mathcal{O}(N\log Nd^{2}W). Applying the ABACUS recurrence costs 𝒪⁡(L​d2​W2)\mathcal{O}(Ld^{2}W^{2}). Thus, ABACUS is generally more efficient when.

N≳Ccache​W​d​(L−1)+CABACUS​W2.\displaystyle N\gtrsim C_{\text{cache}}Wd(L-1)+C_{\text{ABACUS}}W^{2}. (14)

where CC is an implementation-dependent constant; for our code, C≈1/6C\approx 1/6 (see Fig. 3). Efficiency depends quadratically on the non-linearity’s receptive field WW, and linearly on both the embedding dimension dd and layer count LL. Patching can minimize WW by allowing multiple spins to contribute to a single embedding vector. Although this increases the embedding vector size, the trade-off is favorable. While very deep networks are inefficient with ABACUS, they are unnecessary with DysonNet because FFT-based convolutions provide a global receptive field. Very wide networks also reduce efficiency. For these, we recommend giving D⁡(𝝈)D(\bm{\sigma}) a block-diagonal structure in channel space creating a mixture-of-experts like structure. Dividing into blocks of fixed size Δ​d\Delta d implies efficiency when N≳C​W2​Δ​d​(L−1)N\gtrsim CW^{2}\Delta d(L-1) making ABACUS scalable to arbitrary wide networks.

V Implementation of DysonNet

So far we have treated the free propagator G0G_{0} and the coupling vertex D⁡(𝝈)D(\bm{\sigma}) as abstract objects, since our algorithms only require their general properties (linearity for G0G_{0}, locality for DD). The reader is invited to instantiate G0G_{0} and DD with their favorite sequence model, such as CNNs [40], Fourier layers [43, 68], or certain forms of linearized self-attention [61]. Here, we will parametrize G0G_{0} as a state space model and D⁡(𝝈)D(\bm{\sigma}) as a short-range CNN (see Fig 1c).

Parameterizing the Green’s function G(l)G^{(l)}. State space models are a natural choice as they allow to interpret G(l)G^{(l)} as a free propagator. This is consistent with viewing the network as a truncated Dyson series. A state space model is a sequence-to-sequence model where the output is obtained by computing the response of a linear state-evolution equation to the input. We implement a bidirectional state-space model mapping a sequence of 𝒉j→𝒉~j\bm{h}_{j}\to\bm{\tilde{h}}_{j} by evolving the state vector 𝒙j∈ℂs×d\bm{x}_{j}\in\mathbb{C}^{s\times d} via the following discretized differential equation

xj,c\displaystyle x_{j,c}\; =Ac​(xj+1,c+xj−1,c−xj,c)+Bc​hj,c,\displaystyle=\;A_{c}\,(x_{j+1,c}+x_{j-1,c}-x_{j,c})+B_{c}\,h_{j,c},\qquad (15)
h~j,c\displaystyle\tilde{h}_{j,c}\; =Cc​xj,\displaystyle=\;C_{c}\,x_{j}, (16)

where Ac∈ℂs×s,Bc∈ℂ1×s,Cc∈ℂs×1A_{c}\in\mathbb{C}^{s\times s},B_{c}\in\mathbb{C}^{1\times s},C_{c}\in\mathbb{C}^{s\times 1} are the learned state matrices. The first term in (16) is the lattice Laplace operator spreading an excitation. As the system is translationally invariant, the response can be calculated using the Fast Fourier transform 𝒉~=ℱ−1​(G⁡(k)⊙ℱ⁡(𝒉))\bm{\tilde{h}}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\bigl(\,G(k)\;\odot\;\mathcal{F}(\bm{h})\,\bigr) and the Green’s function

Gc​(k)=Cc​(I−ei​2​π​k/N​Ac)−1​Bc.\displaystyle G_{c}(k)=C_{c}\,(I-e^{i2\pi k/N}A_{c})^{-1}B_{c}\;. (17)

When Ac=diag⁡(λ1,…,λs)A_{c}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{s}) is diagonal, the resolvent and G⁡(k)G(k) reduce to a sum of Cauchy kernels (simple poles)

Gc​(k)=∑j=1sCc,j​Bc,j 1−ei​2​π​k/N​λc,j.\displaystyle\;G_{c}(k)\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^{s}\frac{C_{c,j}B_{c,j}}{\,1-e^{i2\pi k/N}\lambda_{c,j}\,}. (18)

Physically, these are damped/oscillatory modes with poles λc,j\lambda_{c,j} inside the unit disk (|λc,j|≤1|\lambda_{c,j}|\leq 1) on the complex plane. The Green’s function corresponds to the free propagation of an excitation (for example domain wall or magnon mode) in space. Note as the number of modes grows, Gc​(k)G_{c}(k) can also approximate power laws over finite range.

In our paper we use the S4 Ansatz for A=Λ+𝒑​𝒒TA=\Lambda+\bm{p}\bm{q}^{T} consisting of a diagonal matrix Λ∈ℂs×s\Lambda\in\mathbb{C}^{s\times s} and a rank one perturbation 𝒑,𝒒∈ℂ1×s\bm{p},\bm{q}\in\mathbb{C}^{1\times s} [24]. We provide the analytical Green’s function G⁡(k)G(k) in appendix J. Making this choice is physically analogous to considering the interacting Green’s function of an excitation scattered at a static impurity.

Parameterizing the local nonlinearity D⁡(𝛔)D(\bm{\sigma}). For parameterizing the local vertex D⁡(𝝈)D(\bm{\sigma}) we use a short-ranged CNN kernel, as this naturally enforces locality via a finite receptive field. From the input configuration we construct a second data stream ϕ(l)\bm{\phi}^{(l)} (see Fig. 1c). Each layer applies (i) a site-wise dense map, (ii) a short-range convolution, and (iii) a nonlinearity. The dense map Dj​(𝝈)D_{j}(\bm{\sigma}) is then conditioned on the data stream ϕ(l)\bm{\phi}^{(l)}

Dj​(𝝈)\displaystyle D_{j}(\bm{\sigma}) =U(l)​diag​(χ⁡(ϕj(l−1)))​V(l).\displaystyle=U^{(l)}\,\mathrm{diag}\!\big(\chi(\bm{\phi}_{j}^{(l-1)})\big)\,V^{(l)}. (19)

Here, χ\chi is a nonlinearity that acts locally on each vector ϕj(l−1)\bm{\phi}_{j}^{(l-1)}. The matrices U(l),V(l)∈ℝd×dU^{(l)},V^{(l)}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} are layer-specific and configuration-independent. Thus Dj​(𝝈)∈ℝd×dD_{j}(\bm{\sigma})\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} has fixed eigenvectors but spin-configuration–dependent eigenvalues through ϕj(l−1)\bm{\phi}^{(l-1)}_{j}. Besides the multiplicative gating D⁡(𝝈)D(\bm{\sigma}) (19) we also inject the ϕj(l)\bm{\phi}_{j}^{(l)} stream into the 𝝈(l)→𝝈(l)+ϕ(l)\bm{\sigma}^{(l)}\to\bm{\sigma}^{(l)}+\bm{\phi}^{(l)} stream via addition before applying the SSM (see Fig. 1c).

VI Benchmarking

We consider the one-dimensional long-range transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) [37, 13]

H=−J𝒩α​(N)∑i≠jσ^iz​σ^jzri​jα−h∑iσ^ix.\displaystyle H=-\,\frac{J}{\mathcal{N}_{\alpha}(N)}\sum_{i\neq j}\frac{\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\hat{\sigma}_{j}^{z}}{r_{ij}^{\alpha}}-h\sum_{i}\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{x}. (20)

where α>0\alpha>0 controls the decay of the Ising interaction, ri​j=min⁡(|i−j|,N−|i−j|)r_{ij}=\min(|i-j|,\,N-|i-j|) is the periodic distance, and 𝒩α​(N)\mathcal{N}_{\alpha}(N) is a Kac factor that keeps the energy density well-defined across α\alpha [13]. We use 𝒩α​(N)=2​∑r=1⌊N/2⌋r−α\mathcal{N}_{\alpha}(N)=2\sum_{r=1}^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}r^{-\alpha}. For J<0J<0 the low-field phase is ferromagnetic; for J>0J>0 it is antiferromagnetic. In the limit α→∞\alpha\to\infty the model reduces to the exactly solvable nearest-neighbor TFIM, diagonalized via the Jordan–Wigner transformation [34, 45, 56]. At α=0\alpha=0 it becomes the fully connected Lipkin–Meshkov–Glick limit [46].

The long-range TFIM spans a diverse set of ground-state behaviors with clean, controllable tuning via α\alpha: (i) for α>3\alpha>3 short-range Ising criticality with universal exponents; (ii) for 5/3<α<35/3<\alpha<3 a genuinely long-range regime with continuously varying, α\alpha-dependent exponents; and (iii) for α<5/3\alpha<5/3 a LR mean-field regime, including dangerous irrelevant variables in finite-size scaling [38]. Away from criticality, long-range couplings generate algebraic (“hybrid exponential–power-law”) correlation tails even in gapped phases, offering a stringent test for variational ansätze to capture both short- and long-distance structure within one architecture [61, 80].

We train all models by minimizing the ground-state energy with Variational Monte-Carlo using stochastic reconfiguration (natural-gradient descent). At each iteration we draw Metropolis samples of spin configurations 𝝈\bm{\sigma} (ABACUS provides O⁡(1)O(1) per-flip amplitudes), estimate the local energy Eloc​(𝝈):=(H​Ψ)​(𝝈)/Ψ⁡(𝝈)E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\bm{\sigma}):=(H\Psi)(\bm{\sigma})/\Psi(\bm{\sigma}) and compute log-derivatives. Parameters are updated as 𝜽←𝜽+η​Δ​𝜽\bm{\theta}\leftarrow\bm{\theta}+\eta\,\Delta\bm{\theta}. Unless noted otherwise, sampler settings, iteration budgets, and solver tolerances are matched across models; detailed training settings are summarized in Appendix Sec. N.

We benchmark DysonNet versus ViT and RBM neural quantum states on the long–range TFIM with system size N=150N=150. ViT represents a highly expressive but expensive Ansatz while RBMs are computationally cheap but less expressive. Training is matched: identical sampler settings, the same system parameters, and an equal budget of 400 iterations. For ViT we adopt the architecture and hyperparameters reported to yield the strongest prior results [61]; for DysonNet we optimize architecture parameters independently while keeping the training protocol identical. We perform two sweeps, JJ at fixed α=4\alpha=4 and α\alpha at fixed J=4.75J=4.75. Each configuration is trained three times with independent initializations and sampler seeds; we report the mean and one standard deviation across three training runs. As a secondary accuracy metric we use the V–score. The V-score, defined as N​Var​(E)/E2N\mathrm{Var}(E)/E^{2}, is a system-size-independent measure of how close the learned state is to an eigenstate. Additional architecture and sampler settings are listed in Appendix Sec. N.

DysonNet achieves substantially lower ground–state energies in the ordered FM and AFM regimes, by 10−210^{-2} to 10−310^{-3} against the ViT. In the paramagnet, ViT is slightly lower, by less than 10−410^{-4}, a scale comparable to typical small–system deviations from the exact energy, so the two are effectively equal. DysonNet consistently outperforms the RBM by at least two orders of magnitude. DysonNet attains consistently smaller V–scores across all parameters, with the largest gains in the short–range AFM regime where the scores improve by up to two orders of magnitude and four orders of magnitude versus the RBM.

We compare wall-clock costs for RBM, ViT, linearized ViT [61], DysonNet, and DysonNet+ABACUS on the TFIM using the protocol of Fig. 2. Because these architectures exhibit different accuracy–compute tradeoffs, panel (a) reports end-to-end training time using the best-performing hyperparameters for each method, i.e., the practical cost of obtaining the best accuracy. Panels (b) and (c) isolate the runtime of the local-estimator and sampler-proposal kernels; matched hyperparameters for this comparison are provided in Appendix Table 3. For fairness, all compared methods are run in TF32 precision and without custom CUDA kernels for ABACUS. Regarding the RBM, Panel (a) displays the NetKet implementation; however, NetKet prioritizes flexibility and does not use specialized local updates for RBMs. Therefore, to test DysonNet+ABACUS against the theoretical limit of RBM performance, we compare the sampler and estimator against custom RBM kernels (violet) that leverage local updates.

As shown in panel (a) of Fig. 3, DysonNet+ABACUS is already strongly advantageous at moderate system sizes: at N=500N=500 spins it trains in 1.5 h, compared to 11.8 h for the directly comparable DysonNet baseline (same model class without ABACUS) and 46.546.5 or 60.160.1 h for the ViT variants. It is also about 2×2\times faster than the RBM baseline 2.9 h at N=500N=500 . We note that our RBM uses NetKet’s general purpose implementation and is not optimized for the best possible constant factors. At N=1000N=1000 the gap to the NetKet RBM becomes substantially larger due to different asymptotic scaling, with DysonNet+ABACUS finishing in 5.29 h versus 25.4 h for the RBM (about a 5×5\times difference), while DysonNet without ABACUS grows to 74.3 h. Importantly, the RBM is not competitive in accuracy. In our setting—its V-score is worse by ∼4\sim 4 orders of magnitude—so it is both markedly less accurate and, at larger NN, slower in wall-clock time.

Panels (b,c) isolate the cost of the two kernels that dominate VMC wall time: evaluating connected matrix elements (local estimator) and proposing single-spin updates. In both cases, DysonNet+ABACUS is the only method with O⁡(1)O(1) cost approximately independent of system size NN. By contrast, DysonNet and RBM updates scale roughly as O⁡(N)O(N), while ViT-style attention scales as O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) over the range shown. At N=1000N=1000, ABACUS yields a 16×16\times (estimator) and 8×8\times (sampler) speedup over the most direct baseline, DysonNet without ABACUS; relative to ViT, the gains are 230×230\times and ∼100×\sim 100\times, respectively. For small systems the RBM kernels are faster because their constants are excellent (one matvec plus a nonlinearity per update), but the linear scaling is eventually overtaken: for sampling, DysonNet+ABACUS becomes faster for N≳340N\gtrsim 340, and for the estimator it becomes more efficient for N≳1000N\gtrsim 1000. Since the RBM is also ∼4\sim 4 orders of magnitude worse in V-score in our setting, DysonNet+ABACUS can outperform this fast-but-inaccurate baseline in both speed and accuracy at larger NN. Absolute speedup factors can shift with hyperparameters and implementations, but the scaling advantage is robust and translates into substantial gains in realistic regimes.

We investigate whether the DysonNet Ansatz accurately captures ground state correlations in large systems where comparison to ED or ViT is impossible. Using ABACUS, we trained DysonNet for α=1.5,2.5,\alpha=1.5,2.5, and 66 in the ferromagnetic phase and extracted critical exponents from finite-size-scaling collapses with PyFSSA [71]. Table 2 lists the extracted critical exponents, and Appendix Figure 7 displays the data collapses. Uncertainties represent the maximum values derived from bootstrap and jackknife methods. We achieve system sizes of N=340N=340 (α=6\alpha=6), N=500N=500 (α=2.5\alpha=2.5), and N=1000N=1000 (α=1.5\alpha=1.5), surpassing the limit of N=150N=150 accessible to ViT [61]. Full training protocol details are provided in Appendix Sec. N.

Table 2 compares the extracted critical points and exponents with exact Stochastic Series Expansion (SSE) benchmarks and with prior Vision Transformer (ViT) results. See also Fig. 7 in the appendix for the collapse plots. DysonNet reproduces the SSE values across all phases. The only appreciable discrepancy is the critical coupling JcJ_{c} at α=1.5\alpha=1.5, where our estimate agrees with ViT rather than SSE. This difference likely arises from either generic biases of Neural Quantum States or a minor mismatch in Hamiltonian normalization. In any case, it is not a concern: JcJ_{c} is non-universal, whereas the universal critical exponents remain correct.

We obtained these results without tuning the nonlinearity width (W=5W=5), network depth (L=2L=2), or proposal spacing (s=10s=10). Holding these parameters fixed indicates that they do not need to scale with system size, even at criticality. As a result, ABACUS supports constant-time local updates for both the sampler and the local estimator. Most importantly, DysonNet improves the ViT estimate of the correlation-length exponent ν\nu at α=1.5\alpha=1.5, yielding ν≈2.04\nu\approx 2.04 instead of ν≈1.6\nu\approx 1.6. This gain in precision comes from our ability to study systems up to N=1000N=1000, well beyond the N≈200N\approx 200 sizes accessible in earlier work [61].

To demonstrate that DysonNet+ABACUS is not tailored to the long-range TFIM, we benchmark the same architecture and local-update machinery in Appendix M on the frustrated antiferromagnetic J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg chain, a standard test for variational wave-function ansätze. This model spans a critical Luttinger-liquid regime and a gapped, spontaneously dimerized phase seperated by a Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition, continuously connecting to the exactly dimerized Majumdar–Ghosh point [53, 18, 84]. In the ED-accessible setting N=20N=20, DysonNet maintains high accuracy across the full sweep achieving an energy error of 10−410^{-4} and a V-score of 10−310^{-3}.

VII Conclusion

We introduce ABACUS, an efficient local update algorithm, and DysonNet, a physically interpretable architecture. ABACUS updates the wavefunction amplitude for any NQS with global linear layers and strictly local non-linearities in 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) time given cached link tensors. Designed for ABACUS, the architecture DysonNet constructs wavefunction amplitudes from local non-linearities connected by global convolutions. It is interpretable as a truncated Dyson series and allows efficient link tensor construction. To amortize caching costs, we employ a screened typewriter sampler that preserves tensors over multiple flips. We derive worst-case runtime bounds and demonstrate a linear speedup. Benchmarks against the long-range transverse-field Ising and frustrated J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} models show that DysonNet matches Vision Transformer accuracy while reducing runtime by two orders of magnitude—an 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) asymptotic improvement. Finally, critical exponent calculations confirm that DysonNet captures correlations at criticality and scales to large systems.

The ABACUS update is straightforwardly compatible with advanced Monte-Carlo strategies, including cluster moves and parallel tempering, opening the door to further runtime improvements [73, 17, 70]. Because the link-tensor construction is agnostic to lattice geometry, DysonNet and ABACUS extend naturally to 2D, inviting applications to the 2D systems [7, 39, 25, 57]. The same structure also accommodates dynamics: DysonNet is compatible with different approaches to time evolution such as the time dependent variational principle [7, 65, 66, 58, 52] or explicitly time dependent NQS [75, 81, 62]. Developing efficient algorithms for link tensor construction beyond the translationally invariant DysonNet case could yield significant efficiency gains for linearized attention in frustrated or disordered phases [26, 2, 59].

Beyond DysonNet, this work points to a general NQS design principle: build long-range correlations by wiring strictly local nonlinearities through global linear layers. This might preserve the expressivity of deep networks while adding algebraic structure that ABACUS can exploit for efficient local updates, pushing variational Monte Carlo to larger system sizes. At the same time, the resulting ansätze admit a diagrammatic interpretation as a scattering series, offering a route to theoretical understanding and characterization via field theory and the renormalization group. We believe this offers a path towards architectures where computational efficiency is enabled by physical interpretability.

Appendix A DysonNet can exactly represent power law decay

For interpreting the DysonNet Ansatz and showing it can express power law decay we will consider the simplifying case of one layer, activation function f⁡(x)=exf(x)=e^{x} and embedding dimension d=1d=1. The log amplitude of the network is

logΨ(𝝈)=AN∑i,jD(σi−w:i+w)Gi−jσj,\displaystyle\log\Psi(\bm{\sigma})=\frac{A}{N}\sum_{i,j}D(\sigma_{i-w:i+w})\,G_{i-j}\sigma_{j}, (21)

To interpret the local vertex we will apply a Fourier-Walsh expansion. Let the window be 𝒲={−w,…,w}\mathcal{W}=\{-w,\dots,w\} with W=2​w+1W=2w+1. Any function D:{±1}W→ℝD:\{\pm 1\}^{W}\to\mathbb{R} has the exact Walsh expansion

D(σi−w:i+w)\displaystyle D(\sigma_{i-w:i+w}) =∑S⊆𝒲DS​∏u∈Sσi+u\displaystyle=\sum_{S\subseteq\mathcal{W}}D_{S}\,\prod_{u\in S}\sigma_{i+u}
=D∅+∑u∈𝒲D{u}​σi+u\displaystyle=D_{\varnothing}+\sum_{u\in\mathcal{W}}D_{\{u\}}\sigma_{i+u} (22)
+∑u<vD{u,v}σi+uσi+v+⋯.\displaystyle+\sum_{u<v}D_{\{u,v\}}\sigma_{i+u}\sigma_{i+v}+\cdots\ .

Inserting (22) into (21) gives

log⁡Ψ=AN​∑S⊆𝒲∑I,jDS​GI−j​(∏u∈Sσi+u)​σj,\displaystyle\log\Psi=\frac{A}{N}\sum_{S\subseteq\mathcal{W}}\sum_{I,j}D_{S}\,G_{I-j}\,\bigg(\prod_{u\in S}\sigma_{i+u}\bigg)\,\sigma_{j}, (23)

so a Walsh monomial of degree |S||S| contributes an interaction of degree |S|+1|S|+1 in the exponent (coupling order).

We first consider the Jastrow limit for W=1W=1. For W=1W=1 (w=0w=0) only S=∅S=\varnothing and S={0}S=\{0\} appear, hence D⁡(σi)=D0+D1​σiD(\sigma_{i})=D_{0}+D_{1}\sigma_{i}. Then (21) reduces to

log⁡Ψ\displaystyle\log\Psi =AN​∑I(D0+D1​σi)​∑jGi−j​σj\displaystyle=\frac{A}{N}\sum_{I}(D_{0}+D_{1}\sigma_{i})\sum_{j}G_{i-j}\sigma_{j}
=h​∑iσi+∑i<jJi​j​σi​σj+const,\displaystyle=h\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}+\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}+\text{const}, (24)

where (for even GrG_{r} and absorbing i=ji=j into the constant)

h=A​D0N​∑rGr,Ji​j=2​A​D1N​G|i−j|.\displaystyle h=\frac{AD_{0}}{N}\sum_{r}G_{r},\qquad J_{ij}=\frac{2AD_{1}}{N}\,G_{|i-j|}\ . (25)
Configuration-sum correlator and small-λ\lambda expansion.

For the W=1W=1 Jastrow limit, diagonal correlators are computed as explicit configuration sums with respect to the induced classical measure p⁡(𝝈)∝|Ψ⁡(𝝈)|2p(\bm{\sigma})\propto|\Psi(\bm{\sigma})|^{2},

⟨σ^iz​σ^i+rz⟩\displaystyle\langle\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\hat{\sigma}_{i+r}^{z}\rangle =1Z​∑𝝈σi​σi+r​exp⁡[ 2​h​∑ℓσℓ+2​∑ℓ<mJℓ​m​σℓ​σm],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{\bm{\sigma}}\sigma_{i}\sigma_{i+r}\,\exp\!\Big[\,2h\sum_{\ell}\sigma_{\ell}+2\sum_{\ell<m}J_{\ell m}\sigma_{\ell}\sigma_{m}\Big], (26)
Z\displaystyle Z =∑𝝈exp⁡[ 2​h​∑ℓσℓ+2​∑ℓ<mJℓ​m​σℓ​σm].\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{\sigma}}\exp\!\Big[\,2h\sum_{\ell}\sigma_{\ell}+2\sum_{\ell<m}J_{\ell m}\sigma_{\ell}\sigma_{m}\Big].

To expose the long-distance scaling we set h=0h=0 (or, equivalently, consider the connected correlator), write Jℓ​m=λ​J¯ℓ​mJ_{\ell m}=\lambda\,\bar{J}_{\ell m}, and expand around λ=0\lambda=0, where the weight becomes uniform. where we expanded the exponential up to second order in the second line. For r≠0r\neq 0 one also has ⟨σi​σi+r⟩0=0\langle\sigma_{i}\sigma_{i+r}\rangle_{0}=0. Moreover, the only non-vanishing four-spin averages are those where the indices pair up; in particular, ⟨σi​σi+r​σℓ​σm⟩0=1\langle\sigma_{i}\sigma_{i+r}\sigma_{\ell}\sigma_{m}\rangle_{0}=1 iff {ℓ,m}={i,i+r}\{\ell,m\}=\{i,i+r\} (and vanishes otherwise). ⟨σi​σi+r⟩=2​λ​J¯i,i+r+O⁡(λ2)=2​Ji,i+r+O⁡(J2).\displaystyle\langle\sigma_{i}\sigma_{i+r}\rangle=2\lambda\,\bar{J}_{i,i+r}+O(\lambda^{2})=2J_{i,i+r}+O(J^{2}). (28)

Using the W=1W=1 identification Ji​j∝G|i−j|J_{ij}\propto G_{|i-j|} and a power-law kernel Gr=r−αG_{r}=r^{-\alpha} therefore yields the leading asymptotic behavior

⟨σi​σi+r⟩=2​Jr+O⁡(J2)∼r−α+O⁡(J2).\displaystyle\langle{\sigma}_{i}{\sigma}_{i+r}\rangle=2J_{r}+O(J^{2})\sim r^{-\alpha}+O(J^{2}). (29)

Higher orders in λ\lambda correspond to multi-edge contributions (paths and graphs) and dress the prefactor, while the leading long-distance tail is set by the direct long-range coupling inherited from GrG_{r}.

For W>1W>1, higher Walsh sectors DSD_{S} in (22) generate controlled multi-spin vertices of order |S|+1|S|{+}1 via (23), adding non-Gaussian short-range dressing beyond a pure Jastrow factor. Stacking LL DysonNet blocks increases the effective coupling order through the Dyson-series structure of repeated D⁡(𝝈)​GD(\bm{\sigma})G insertions, while preserving the separation of scales: GG fixes the long-distance response (e.g. algebraic kernels suitable for criticality) and DD learns non-universal local structure. Allowing complex parameters further enables nontrivial sign/phase structure beyond strictly positive Jastrow states.

In this section we prove Theorem I and the recursion relations (10) and (11) via induction. For a local update 𝝈=𝝈0+Δ​𝝈\bm{\sigma}=\bm{\sigma}_{0}+\Delta\bm{\sigma}, define

ℳ⁡(𝝈)\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\bm{\sigma}) :=∏l=1L(D0(l)+Δ​D(l))​M(l),\displaystyle:=\prod_{l=1}^{L}\!\bigl(D^{(l)}_{0}+\Delta D^{(l)}\bigr)M^{(l)}, (30)
𝛀⁡(𝝈)\displaystyle\bm{\Omega}(\bm{\sigma}) =A​PM​ℳ​(𝝈)​𝝈.\displaystyle=A\,P_{M}\,\mathcal{M}(\bm{\sigma})\,\bm{\sigma}. (31)

A matrix word is one summand in the expansion of ℳ⁡(𝝈)\mathcal{M}(\bm{\sigma}). Its pivot is the largest layer index ll for which Δ​D(l)\Delta D^{(l)} appears. Let 𝒲l\mathcal{W}_{l} be the set of words with pivot ll, and define

𝒉~(l):=PS,j​∑W∈𝒲lW​𝝈∈ℝW×d.\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(l)}:=P_{S,j}\sum_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{l}}W\,\bm{\sigma}\quad\in\mathbb{R}^{W\times d}. (32)
Invariant 1 (after line 3 of Algorithm II).

For every l≤Ll\leq L, the recursion (10) equals the sum over all words with pivot ll.

𝒉~(l)=PS,j​∑W∈𝒲lW​𝝈.\bm{\tilde{h}}^{(l)}=P_{S,j}\sum_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{l}}W\,\bm{\sigma}\;. (33)

Proof. We use strong induction over ll.

Base case l=1l=1.

For pivot 11, the only scattering layer is the first one.

𝒉~(1)\displaystyle\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(1)} =PS,j​Δ​D(1)​M(1)​(𝝈0+Δ​𝝈)\displaystyle=P_{S,j}\,\Delta D^{(1)}M^{(1)}(\bm{\sigma}_{0}+\Delta\bm{\sigma})
=Δ​D(1)​(M(1)​Δ​𝝈+𝒉~0(1)),\displaystyle=\Delta D^{(1)}\!\left(M^{(1)}\Delta\bm{\sigma}+\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(1)}_{0}\right), (34)

which is exactly the initialization in Algorithm II.

Induction step. Assume (33) holds for all k<lk<l. Any word with pivot ll is obtained by applying Δ​D(l)​M(l)\Delta D^{(l)}M^{(l)} to either: (i) the unscattered incident field at layer ll, or (ii) a word with pivot m<lm<l, propagated from mm to ll through background factors D0(n)​M(n)D_{0}^{(n)}M^{(n)}, n=m+1,…,l−1n=m+1,\dots,l-1. Therefore,

∑W∈𝒲lW​𝝈\displaystyle\sum_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{l}}W\bm{\sigma} =ΔD(l)M(l)[𝒉0(l)\displaystyle=\Delta D^{(l)}M^{(l)}\bigg[\bm{h}^{(l)}_{0} (35)
+∑m=1l−1(∏n=m+1l−1D0(n)M(n))∑W∈𝒲mW𝝈].\displaystyle+\sum_{m=1}^{l-1}\left(\prod_{n=m+1}^{l-1}D_{0}^{(n)}M^{(n)}\right)\sum_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{m}}W\bm{\sigma}\bigg].

Projecting to the slice and using the induction hypothesis gives

𝒉~(l)=Δ​D(l)​(M~(l)​𝒉~(l−1)+∑m=1l−2L(l,m)​𝒉~(m)+𝒉~0(l)),\displaystyle\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(l)}=\Delta D^{(l)}\!\left(\tilde{M}^{(l)}\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(l-1)}+\sum_{m=1}^{l-2}L^{(l,m)}\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(m)}+\tilde{\bm{h}}_{0}^{(l)}\right), (36)

where L(l,m)L^{(l,m)} is exactly the link tensor from Eq. (9).

L(l,m)=PS,j​M(l)​(∏n=m+1l−1D0(n)​M(n))​PS,j⊤.\displaystyle L^{(l,m)}=P_{S,j}M^{(l)}\left(\prod_{n=m+1}^{l-1}D_{0}^{(n)}M^{(n)}\right)P_{S,j}^{\top}. (37)

This is Eq. (10), so the invariant is preserved.

Termination: After the loop (l=Ll=L), (33) holds for every pivot class. Grouping the full expansion by pivot and contracting each class with its output link tensor T(l)T^{(l)} yields

𝛀⁡(𝝈)=A⁡(PM​𝒉~(L)+∑l=1LT(l)​𝒉~(l)),\displaystyle\bm{\Omega}(\bm{\sigma})=A\!\left(P_{M}\,\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(L)}+\sum_{l=1}^{L}T^{(l)}\tilde{\bm{h}}^{(l)}\right), (38)

which is Eq. (11). Hence ABACUS produces the desired matrix-vector product exactly.

Complexity. Using only the principal blocks of the Toeplitz matrix, contracting a vector 𝒉~(l)\bm{\tilde{h}}^{(l)} with G(l)G^{(l)} and then applying the slice projection PS,jP_{S,j} requires 𝒪⁡(d​W2)\mathcal{O}\!\left(d\,W^{2}\right) operations, where W=2​w+1≪NW=2w+1\ll N denotes the slice width and dd is the hidden‐state dimension. If WW becomes large, the same contraction can instead be performed with a state-space model (SSM) in 𝒪⁡(W​d​s2)\mathcal{O}(W\,d\,s^{2}) time, which scales strictly linearly in WW.

Multiplying 𝒉~(l)\bm{\tilde{h}}^{(l)} by the sparse diagonal update Δ​D(l)\Delta D^{(l)} costs 𝒪⁡(W​d2)\mathcal{O}\!\left(W\,d^{2}\right), again linear in the slice width. The link tensors at the final layer, T(l)T^{(l)}, incur the same 𝒪⁡(W​d2)\mathcal{O}\!\left(W\,d^{2}\right) cost, while the most expensive step is contracting with the multi-layer link tensors, which scales as 𝒪⁡(W2​d2)\mathcal{O}\!\left(W^{2}\,d^{2}\right) yet remains independent of the full system size NN.

Since every individual contraction is free of any NN-dependence, the entire update can be carried out in constant time with respect to NN. For a network of LL layers, roughly L⁡(L−1)/2∼𝒪⁡(L2)L(L-1)/2\sim\mathcal{O}(L^{2}) such contractions are required, giving the overall worst-case complexity 𝒪⁡(d2​W2​L2),\mathcal{O}\!\bigl(d^{2}W^{2}L^{2}\bigr), which is constant in NN and quadratic in both the number of layers and the slice width.

By a strong-induction loop-invariant argument we have shown that Algorithm II constructs every matrix word exactly once, associates it with the correct pre-contracted linear environment, and thus evaluates the network output 𝛀⁡(𝝈)\bm{\Omega}(\bm{\sigma}) at 𝒪⁡(d2​W2​L2)\mathcal{O}(d^{2}W^{2}L^{2}) constant in NN cost for a local spin flip. ■\blacksquare

Appendix C Screened Metropolis sampler is exact

Let π⁡(𝝈)∝|Ψ⁡(𝝈)|2\pi(\bm{\sigma})\propto|\Psi(\bm{\sigma})|^{2} be the target distribution and consider a symmetric proposal q⁡(𝝈→𝝈′)=q⁡(𝝈′→𝝈)q(\bm{\sigma}\to\bm{\sigma}^{\prime})=q(\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}\to\bm{\sigma}). Define the exact Metropolis–Hastings ratio

R⁡(𝝈,𝝈′):=|Ψ⁡(𝝈′)|2|Ψ⁡(𝝈)|2,α⁡(𝝈→𝝈′):=min⁡{1,R⁡(𝝈,𝝈′)}.R(\bm{\sigma},\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}):=\frac{|\Psi(\bm{\sigma}^{\prime})|^{2}}{|\Psi(\bm{\sigma})|^{2}},\qquad\alpha(\bm{\sigma}\to\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}):=\min\{1,R(\bm{\sigma},\bm{\sigma}^{\prime})\}. (39)

Assume we can compute deterministic bounds L⁡(𝝈,𝝈′)L(\bm{\sigma},\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}) and U⁡(𝝈,𝝈′)U(\bm{\sigma},\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}) such that

L⁡(𝝈,𝝈′)≤R⁡(𝝈,𝝈′)≤U⁡(𝝈,𝝈′)for all ​(𝝈,𝝈′).L(\bm{\sigma},\bm{\sigma}^{\prime})\leq R(\bm{\sigma},\bm{\sigma}^{\prime})\leq U(\bm{\sigma},\bm{\sigma}^{\prime})\qquad\text{for all }(\bm{\sigma},\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}). (40)

Consider the screened acceptance rule: draw u∼𝒰⁡[0,1]u\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1] and (i) accept if u<min⁡{1,L}u<\min\{1,L\}; (ii) reject if u>min⁡{1,U}u>\min\{1,U\}; (iii) otherwise (the ambiguous window) compute RR exactly and accept iff u<min⁡{1,R}u<\min\{1,R\}. Then the resulting accept/reject decision coincides with the standard MH decision for every triple (𝝈,𝝈′,u)(\bm{\sigma},\bm{\sigma}^{\prime},u), hence the induced Markov chain satisfies detailed balance with respect to π\pi and is exact.

Proof. By (40) we have min⁡{1,L}≤min⁡{1,R}≤min⁡{1,U}\min\{1,L\}\leq\min\{1,R\}\leq\min\{1,U\}. If u<min⁡{1,L}u<\min\{1,L\} then u<min⁡{1,R}u<\min\{1,R\} and both screened MH and MH accept. If u>min⁡{1,U}u>\min\{1,U\} then u>min⁡{1,R}u>\min\{1,R\} and both reject. Otherwise u∈[min⁡{1,L},min⁡{1,U}]u\in[\min\{1,L\},\min\{1,U\}] and the screened rule evaluates RR and applies the MH test u<min⁡{1,R}u<\min\{1,R\}, which is exactly the MH decision. Therefore the transition kernel is identical to MH, and detailed balance π⁡(𝝈)​q​(𝝈→𝝈′)​α​(𝝈→𝝈′)=π⁡(𝝈′)​q​(𝝈′→𝝈)​α​(𝝈′→𝝈)\pi(\bm{\sigma})q(\bm{\sigma}\to\bm{\sigma}^{\prime})\alpha(\bm{\sigma}\to\bm{\sigma}^{\prime})=\pi(\bm{\sigma}^{\prime})q(\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}\to\bm{\sigma})\alpha(\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}\to\bm{\sigma}) holds. ∎

Appendix E Sampling Complexity

We model premature freezing of an approximate Metropolis chain via a step–dependent stop (“hazard”) probability (see also Ref. [1, 35]). The objective is to compute the expected number of successful moves before the chain either freezes or reaches a deterministic cap. At the kk-th attempted local flip (k=1,2,…k=1,2,\dots) the chain freezes with probability

pk=p0​kγ,γ≥0,p_{k}\;=\;p_{0}\,k^{\gamma},\qquad\gamma\geq 0, (71)

otherwise it proceeds to k+1k{+}1. Independently of freezing, the chain is capped after

K=Nw=N 1−βw0,w⁡(N)=w0​Nβ,  0≤β≤1,K\;=\;\frac{N}{w}\;=\;\frac{N^{\,1-\beta}}{w_{0}},\qquad w(N)=w_{0}N^{\beta},\;\;0\leq\beta\leq 1, (72)

accepted moves. We denote by MM the number of accepted flips before the first of freeze or cap occurs, and we seek 𝔼⁡[M]\mathbb{E}[M].

General hazard results

Exact expression.

Survival through step kk requires not freezing in any of the steps 1,…,k1,\dots,k. Thus

Pr⁡(M≥k)=∏i=1k(1−p0​iγ),k≤K,\Pr(M\geq k)\;=\;\prod_{i=1}^{k}\!\big(1-p_{0}\,i^{\gamma}\big),\qquad k\leq K, (73)

and by the tail–sum formula

𝔼⁡[M]=∑k=1K∏i=1k(1−p0​iγ).\;\mathbb{E}[M]\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}\;\prod_{i=1}^{k}\!\big(1-p_{0}\,i^{\gamma}\big)\;. (74)

(If p0​iγ≥1p_{0}\,i^{\gamma}\geq 1 for some ii, the product—and thus all later terms—vanishes.)

When p0​iγ≪1p_{0}i^{\gamma}\ll 1 up to the relevant ii, we use log⁡(1−x)≈−x\log(1-x)\approx-x and ∑i=1kiγ≈kγ+1/(γ+1)\sum_{i=1}^{k}i^{\gamma}\approx k^{\gamma+1}/(\gamma{+}1) to obtain

𝔼⁡[M]≈∑k=1Kexp⁡(−p0γ+1​kγ+1)≈∫0Ke−a​tγ+1​𝑑t,\mathbb{E}[M]\;\approx\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}\!\exp\!\Big(-\frac{p_{0}}{\gamma+1}k^{\gamma+1}\Big)\;\approx\;\int_{0}^{K}e^{-at^{\gamma+1}}\,dt, (75)

with a:=p0/(γ+1)a:=p_{0}/(\gamma+1). Define the hazard length

ℓ:=a−1/(γ+1)=(γ+1p0)1/(γ+1)\;\ell:=a^{-1/(\gamma+1)}\;=\;\Big(\frac{\gamma+1}{p_{0}}\Big)^{\!1/(\gamma+1)}\; (76)

at which the cumulative hazard is O⁡(1)O(1). Comparing ℓ\ell to the cap KK in (72) yields two regimes:

Hazard-limited (K≫ℓK\gg\ell): the integral in (75) saturates,

𝔼[M]∼Cγp0−1/(γ+1),Cγ=Γ⁡(1γ+1)(γ+1)γ/(γ+1)\;\mathbb{E}[M]\;\sim\;C_{\gamma}\,p_{0}^{-1/(\gamma+1)},\qquad C_{\gamma}=\frac{\Gamma\!\big(\tfrac{1}{\gamma+1}\big)}{(\gamma+1)^{\gamma/(\gamma+1)}}\; (77)

Cap-limited (K≪ℓK\ll\ell): freezing is negligible before the cap,

𝔼⁡[M]∼K=Nw\;\mathbb{E}[M]\;\sim\;K\;=\;\frac{N}{w}\; (78)

The crossover is conveniently expressed as

p0​Kγ+1∼ 1,p_{0}\,K^{\gamma+1}\;\sim\;1, (79)

equivalently K∼ℓK\sim\ell by (76).

Exponentially decaying correlations (area law).

A standard bound gives an error per window of the form ϵ≲Ce−w/ξw−1(k/K)\epsilon\lesssim C\,e^{-w/\xi}\,w^{-1}(k/K), suggesting a linear hazard γ=1\gamma=1 with

pk=p0k,p0∼Ce−w/ξ.p_{k}=p_{0}k,\qquad p_{0}\sim Ce^{-w/\xi}. (80)

To keep the error in (80) controlled, we can rescale the minimum spacing logarithmically with NN by setting w⁡(N)=w0​log⁡Nw(N)=w_{0}\log N. Comparing KK and ℓ\ell,

Kℓ∼N 1−w0/(2​ξ)log⁡N,\frac{K}{\ell}\;\sim\;\frac{N^{\,1-w_{0}/(2\xi)}}{\log N}\,, (81)

so one crosses from hazard- to cap-limited as w0w_{0} increases. In particular, for sufficiently large w0w_{0} (e.g. w0>2​ξw_{0}>2\xi in our conservative criterion), the chain is cap-limited and by (78)

𝔼⁡[M]∼Nw0​log⁡N,\;\mathbb{E}[M]\;\sim\;\frac{N}{w_{0}\log N}\;, (82)

yielding quasi-linear sampling per pass, 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(N\log N).

Weak long-range power law (α>1\alpha>1; resummable tail).

The mean-field error bound gives a linear hazard (γ=1\gamma=1) with a window–controlled prefactor

p0∼Cwα,α>1.p_{0}\sim\frac{C}{w^{\alpha}},\qquad\alpha>1. (83)

The associated hazard length is ℓ∼p0−1/2∼wα/2\ell\sim p_{0}^{-1/2}\sim w^{\alpha/2}. Let the window scale as w⁡(N)=w0​Nβw(N)=w_{0}N^{\beta}, and recall the cap size

K∼Nw∼N1−β.K\sim\frac{N}{w}\sim N^{1-\beta}. (84)

When K≫ℓK\gg\ell, the process freezes from the hazard before hitting the cap, and

𝔼[M]∼ℓ∼p0−1/2∼Nα​β2.\mathbb{E}[M]\;\sim\;\ell\;\sim\;p_{0}^{-1/2}\;\sim\;N^{\frac{\alpha\beta}{2}}. (85)

This increases monotonically with β\beta (a larger window suppresses the hazard, allowing more accepted flips). When K≪ℓK\ll\ell, the chain almost never freezes early and runs to the cap,

𝔼⁡[M]∼K∼Nw∼N1−β.\mathbb{E}[M]\;\sim\;K\;\sim\;\frac{N}{w}\;\sim\;N^{1-\beta}. (86)

This decreases monotonically with β\beta (a larger window lowers the cap).

Since the hazard-limited value grows with β\beta while the cap-limited value shrinks with β\beta, the optimum is attained precisely at the crossover where the two branches match.

N1−β∼Nα2​β⟹βc=22+α.N^{1-\beta}\;\sim\;N^{\frac{\alpha}{2}\beta}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\,\beta_{c}=\frac{2}{2+\alpha}\,. (87)

At this βc\beta_{c}, the two expressions (85) and (86) coincide and yield

𝔼​[M]opt∼N1−βc=Nα2+α.\,\mathbb{E}[M]_{\mathrm{opt}}\;\sim\;N^{1-\beta_{c}}\;=\;N^{\frac{\alpha}{2+\alpha}}\,. (88)

Pairwise-dominated cross terms yield a superlinear hazard

pk=p0​kγ,γ=2−α>1,p0∼C~wα,p_{k}=p_{0}\,k^{\gamma},\qquad\gamma=2-\alpha>1,\qquad p_{0}\sim\frac{\tilde{C}}{w^{\alpha}}, (89)

Let w⁡(N)=w0​Nβw(N)=w_{0}N^{\beta} and recall the cap (84), K∼N1−βK\sim N^{1-\beta}. If K≫ℓK\gg\ell, the process freezes before the cap, and by analogy with (85) one has

𝔼[M]∼ℓ∼p0−1/(3−α)∼wα/(3−α)∼Nα​β3−α.\mathbb{E}[M]\;\sim\;\ell\;\sim\;p_{0}^{-1/(3-\alpha)}\;\sim\;w^{\alpha/(3-\alpha)}\;\sim\;N^{\frac{\alpha\beta}{3-\alpha}}. (90)

This increases monotonically with β\beta (a larger window suppresses the hazard more strongly).

If K≪ℓK\ll\ell, the chain essentially always reaches the cap, just as in (86).

𝔼⁡[M]∼K∼Nw∼N1−β.\mathbb{E}[M]\;\sim\;K\;\sim\;\frac{N}{w}\;\sim\;N^{1-\beta}. (91)

This decreases monotonically with β\beta (a larger window lowers the cap).

Because the hazard-limited value rises with β\beta while the cap-limited value falls with β\beta, the optimum is achieved at the crossover, exactly as argued in (87). Equating the two scalings gives

βc=3−α3.\,\beta_{c}=\frac{3-\alpha}{3}\,. (92)

At β=βc\beta=\beta_{c}, the branches (90) and (91) coincide, yielding

𝔼​[M]opt∼N 1−βc=Nα/3.\,\mathbb{E}[M]_{\mathrm{opt}}\;\sim\;N^{\,1-\beta_{c}}\;=\;N^{\alpha/3}\,. (93)
