Plugging α=0\alpha=0 into (92) gives βc=1\beta_{c}=1, i.e. w∝Nw\propto N so K∼N/wK\sim N/w is constant. Correspondingly, (93) gives 𝔼​[M]opt∼N0\mathbb{E}[M]_{\mathrm{opt}}\sim N^{0}: there is no asymptotic sampling advantage in the fully connected (α=0\alpha=0) case, although constant-factor speedups (from better constants in p0p_{0} or reduced autocorrelation) can still be realized in practice.

Appendix F Practical implementation of the screened typewriter sampler

Implementing the screened typewriter sampler on GPUs requires modifying Algorithm 2 to maximize parallelism. We process proposals for an entire batch of chains simultaneously. Because the Independent Scattering Approximation (ISA) renders defects non-interacting, we parallelize computationally intensive steps—such as link tensor construction and ABACUS recurrence—both across chains and across the proposals within a single chain. With amplitudes precomputed, a lightweight loop handles acceptance. To accommodate the limited control flow of GPUs, we do not halt execution when a chain freezes; instead, we use masking to prevent updates to the output buffer, preserving batch synchronization. Optimizing this masking scheme could yield further speedups.

The screened typewriter sampler requires exact error bounds to remain exact. These bounds can be computed by evaluating Eq. (59) and Eq. (50), which guarantees that the screened typewriter sampler is provably unbiased. Additionally, we provide a pragmatic strategy that is easier to implement than evaluating Eq. (50) at every step. We allocate a buffer ϵ⁡(k)\epsilon(k) indexed by the number of accepted flips kk. We initialize ϵ⁡(k)\epsilon(k) to a conservative value (e.g., 0.2) to ensure it exceeds the actual error, thereby forcing the chain to freeze prematurely. During these freeze events, we obtain the empirical error ϵ~\tilde{\epsilon} at no additional computational overhead by comparing the exact and approximate acceptance ratios. If ϵ⁡(k)\epsilon(k) retains its initial default value, we overwrite it with ϵ~\tilde{\epsilon}; otherwise, we update ϵ⁡(k)←max⁡{ϵ⁡(k),γ​ϵ~}\epsilon(k)\leftarrow\max\{\epsilon(k),\gamma\tilde{\epsilon}\} with γ>1\gamma>1. This heuristic converges rapidly, self-corrects as the wavefunction evolves, and avoids calibration parameters. We note, however, that it is still a heuristic and can underestimate ϵ⁡(k)\epsilon(k) early in training, which may introduce bias. For this reason, we discard the first few sweeps at the beginning of each training run. Empirically, after this burn-in, the error bounds are accurate and the sampler satisfies the Metropolis–Hastings rule exactly. All final observables we report (ground-state energy, observables, V-score, etc.) are obtained with a provably exact sampler.

Figure S5 plots the average sampler throughput of the screened typewriter scheme. Throughput is defined as the average number of proposals per chain between cache refreshes. Since link-tensor construction is the expensive 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(N\log N) step, this metric quantifies how well the scheme amortizes that cost.

A dashed line marks the ideal case, where screening never triggers during a pass. With block spacing WW, a pass contains

Mideal​(N)=N2​W.M_{\rm ideal}(N)\;=\;\frac{N}{2W}. (94)

proposals per chain, yielding the linear reference.

We examine models trained at α=1.5\alpha=1.5. This setting poses the greatest challenge: long-range correlations reduce the accuracy of the independent-scattering approximation (ISA). Nevertheless, throughput scales linearly with NN, tracking the ideal line. The curves diverge only at the largest system size (N=1000N=1000), signaling premature freezing. Here, screening triggers early, forcing a cache refresh before the cap is complete. Even in this regime, the sampler retains 80–90% of the ideal throughput.

Consequently, we keep WW constant. The linear scaling demonstrates that fixed spacing efficiently amortizes cache costs. The throughput drop at N=1000N=1000 does not justify increasing WW; adjusting the interval width becomes necessary only for N>1000N>1000.

Finally, the figure reveals the sampler’s sensitivity to ground-state correlations. Throughput peaks in the ferromagnetic and paramagnetic regimes but falls near the critical point, Jc≈−1.4J_{c}\approx-1.4. There, long-range correlations increase ISA interference, forcing proposals into the ambiguous window and triggering early cache refreshes.

Appendix G Efficient construction of link tensors

Final-stage links T(l)T^{(l)}. The final-stage link tensors T(l)T^{(l)} only have rank dd. They can therefore be computed using dd reverse matrix vector products. In all machine learning libraries this can be computed highly efficiently via dd backwards passes.

Two-layer links L(l,l−1)L^{(l,l-1)}. The two-layer link tensors Lj,Δ​j(l,l−1)L^{(l,l-1)}_{j,\Delta j} can be efficiently computed using convolutions. Specifically, we have

Lj,Δ​j(l,l−1)\displaystyle L^{(l,l-1)}_{j,\Delta j} =∑k𝑮j+Δ​j−k(l)​Dk(l−1)​𝑮k−j(l−1).\displaystyle=\sum_{k}\bm{G}_{j+\Delta j-k}^{(l)}D_{k}^{(l-1)}\bm{G}_{k-j}^{(l-1)}\ . (95)

Let’s define the composite Green’s function G~j−k,Δ​j(l)=𝑮j−k+Δ​j⊗𝑮−(j−k){\tilde{G}}_{j-k,\Delta j}^{(l)}=\bm{G}_{j-k+\Delta j}\otimes\bm{G}_{-(j-k)}. This is another convolution kernel meaning we can efficiently construct the link tensor via the matrix valued FFT

Lj,Δ​j(l,l−1)=ℱ−1​(ℱ⁡(G~Δ​j(l))⊙ℱ⁡(D(l−1)))|j.\displaystyle L^{(l,l-1)}_{j,\Delta j}=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\mathcal{F}(\tilde{G}_{\Delta j}^{(l)})\odot\mathcal{F}(D^{(l-1)}))|_{j}\ . (96)

We need this link tensor for all j∈{1,…,N}j\in\{1,\dots,N\} but for Δ​j∈{−w,…,w+1}\Delta j\in\{-w,\dots,w+1\}. This means the link tensor can be constructed in 𝒪⁡(d2​W​N​log⁡N)⊂𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(d^{2}WN\log N)\subset\mathcal{O}(N\log N).

Multi-layer links |l−m|≥3|l-m|\geq 3. Direct nested FFTs scale as badly for more than two layers. We can instead use randomized SVDs to obtain the link tensors L(l,m)≈U(l,m)​Σ~k(l,m)​V(l,m)L^{(l,m)}\approx U^{(l,m)}\,\tilde{\Sigma}^{(l,m)}_{k}\,V^{(l,m)} using k≪W​dk\ll Wd random probes (linear-time in NN for fixed kk) and a small 𝒪⁡(k3)\mathcal{O}(k^{3}) factorization on slice-shaped matrices. In the worst case k=W​dk=Wd this incurs a total cost of 𝒪⁡(W​d2​N​log⁡N+W​d3​N)⊂𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(Wd^{2}N\log N+Wd^{3}N)\subset\mathcal{O}(N\log N) matrix vector multiplication cost and 𝒪⁡(W3​d3)\mathcal{O}(W^{3}d^{3}) build cost. Note using randomized SVDs the error can be made arbitrarily small. Nevertheless, in this paper we empirically only need two layers to obtain accurate results. Therefore, we do not require this construction, meaning the ABACUS algorithm returns provably exact results without controlling for error.

Appendix H Exact algorithm to construct link tensors for arbitrary network depth

In our benchmarks, two layers of DysonNet suffice for high performance, allowing us to construct all link tensors efficiently using FFTs. However, because nested FFT contraction scales poorly with depth, this strategy fails for deeper networks. To demonstrate that ABACUS is mathematically exact and asymptotically efficient, we provide an advanced algorithm for constructing link tensors, even though our experiments do not require it.

We leverage additional structure in the long-range token mixer to compute link tensors efficiently. Consistent with our assumption that long-wavelength propagation is controlled by only a few modes, we model each Green’s-function mixer G(ℓ)∈ℝN×NG^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} as a hierarchical off-diagonal low-rank (HODLR) matrix. HODLR matrix multplication is highly efficient allowing us to build the link tensors at reasonable cost. We show that SSM impulse-response kernels (finite sums of exponentials) are exactly HODLR.

H.1 Definition of HODLR matrices

Fix an ordering of token indices {1,…,N}\{1,\dots,N\} along a 1D chain (or along a chosen space-filling order in higher dimensions), so that contiguous index sets correspond to local spatial neighborhoods. For simplicity assume N=2pN=2^{p} and define a recursive binary partition of the index interval into contiguous halves. At the top level,

I1:={1,…,N/2},I2:={N/2+1,…,N}.I_{1}:=\{1,\dots,N/2\},\qquad I_{2}:=\{N/2+1,\dots,N\}. (97)
Definition II (HODLR matrix).

A matrix A∈ℝN×NA\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} is HODLR of rank ≤r\leq r (with leaf size n0n_{0}) if it can be represented as

A=(AI1,I1AI1,I2AI2,I1AI2,I2),AI1,I2=U12​V12⊤,AI2,I1=U21​V21⊤,\displaystyle A\;=\;\begin{pmatrix}A_{I_{1},I_{1}}&A_{I_{1},I_{2}}\\[2.0pt] A_{I_{2},I_{1}}&A_{I_{2},I_{2}}\end{pmatrix},A_{I_{1},I_{2}}=U_{12}V_{12}^{\top},\quad A_{I_{2},I_{1}}=U_{21}V_{21}^{\top}, (98)

where rank⁡(AI1,I2),rank⁡(AI2,I1)≤r\mathrm{rank}(A_{I_{1},I_{2}}),\mathrm{rank}(A_{I_{2},I_{1}})\leq r, and where the diagonal blocks AI1,I1A_{I_{1},I_{1}} and AI2,I2A_{I_{2},I_{2}} are again HODLR of rank ≤r\leq r under the next binary split of I1I_{1} and I2I_{2}, recursively, until blocks reach size ≤n0\leq n_{0} (stored densely). Importantly, only the diagonal blocks are refined recursively; off-diagonal blocks are stored as low-rank factors at the level where they appear.

H.2 SSM kernels are exactly HODLR

Consider a 1D translation-invariant Green’s function (Toeplitz kernel)

Gi​j=g⁡(|i−j|),i,j∈{1,…,N}.G_{ij}\;=\;g(|i-j|),\qquad i,j\in\{1,\dots,N\}. (99)

We focus on SSM impulse responses, which in real space are finite sums of (possibly damped/oscillatory) modes. For clarity we first treat real exponentials, then state the extension.

Proposition III (Sum of exponentials ⇒\Rightarrow exact low-rank off-diagonal blocks).

Let

g⁡(t)=∑p=1sαp​λpt,|λp|<1.g(t)=\sum_{p=1}^{s}\alpha_{p}\lambda_{p}^{t},\qquad|\lambda_{p}|<1. (100)

Let I={a,…,b}I=\{a,\dots,b\} and J={c,…,d}J=\{c,\dots,d\} be two disjoint contiguous index intervals with b<cb<c (i.e. II lies strictly to the left of JJ). Then the off-diagonal block GI,JG_{I,J} has rank at most ss and factors as

GI,J=∑p=1suI(p)​(vJ(p))⊤,uI(p)​(i)=λp−i,vJ(p)​(j)=αp​λpj.G_{I,J}\;=\;\sum_{p=1}^{s}u^{(p)}_{I}\bigl(v^{(p)}_{J}\bigr)^{\top},\qquad u^{(p)}_{I}(i)=\lambda_{p}^{-i},\quad v^{(p)}_{J}(j)=\alpha_{p}\,\lambda_{p}^{j}. (101)

The analogous statement holds for blocks strictly below the diagonal. In particular, for any recursive binary partition into contiguous halves (Definition II), every off-diagonal block is exactly rank ≤s\leq s, hence GG is an exact HODLR matrix with rank bound r≤sr\leq s.

Proof.

If i∈Ii\in I and j∈Jj\in J with i<ji<j, then |i−j|=j−i|i-j|=j-i and

Gi​j=∑p=1sαp​λpj−i=∑p=1s(λp−i)​(αp​λpj),G_{ij}=\sum_{p=1}^{s}\alpha_{p}\lambda_{p}^{j-i}=\sum_{p=1}^{s}\bigl(\lambda_{p}^{-i}\bigr)\bigl(\alpha_{p}\lambda_{p}^{j}\bigr), (102)

which is precisely the separable expansion in Eq. (101). ∎

Remark IV (Damped oscillations / complex poles).

Many SSM kernels are sums of damped oscillatory modes corresponding to complex poles inside the unit disk. Writing such modes as complex exponentials (or equivalently as real exp(−t/ξ)cos(ωt)\exp(-t/\xi)\cos(\omega t) and exp(−t/ξ)sin(ωt)\exp(-t/\xi)\sin(\omega t) pairs) preserves the same separability argument; the exact HODLR rank bound is proportional to the number of modes (counting complex-conjugate pairs appropriately).

H.3 Link tensor construction

Let the network have depth LL with layers indexed by ℓ=1,…,L\ell=1,\dots,L. Let D(ℓ)​(𝝈0)D^{(\ell)}(\bm{\sigma}_{0}) denote the frozen-background diagonal (local) vertex at layer ℓ\ell (see main text), and let G(ℓ)G^{(\ell)} be the corresponding Green’s-function token mixer. Define the composite layer operator

B(ℓ)\displaystyle B^{(\ell)} :=D(ℓ)​(𝝈0)​G(ℓ).\displaystyle:=D^{(\ell)}(\bm{\sigma}_{0})\,G^{(\ell)}. (103)

For integers 1≤a≤b≤L1\leq a\leq b\leq L, define the consecutive product

Xa,b\displaystyle X_{a,b} :=B(a)B(a+1)⋯B(b),Xa,a=B(a),\displaystyle:=B^{(a)}B^{(a+1)}\cdots B^{(b)},\qquad X_{a,a}=B^{(a)}, (104)

and use the convention

Xa,b\displaystyle X_{a,b} :=I(a>b).\displaystyle:=I\qquad(a>b). (105)

Let PS,jP_{S,j} be the projector onto the local patch SjS_{j} (width WW) centered at site jj. For any pair of layers ℓ>m\ell>m, we cache the local interlayer link tensor as the patch-restricted block

ℒj(ℓ,m)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{(\ell,m)}_{j} :=PS,j​(G(ℓ)​Xm+1,ℓ−1)​PS,j⊤∈ℝd​W×d​W.\displaystyle:=P_{S,j}\,\Bigl(G^{(\ell)}\,X_{m+1,\ell-1}\Bigr)\,P_{S,j}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{dW\times dW}. (106)

For ℓ=m+1\ell=m+1, the segment is empty and Eq. (105) gives Xm+1,ℓ−1=IX_{m+1,\ell-1}=I.

H.4 Parallel construction via scans

The previous section outlined how to construct the link tensors using HODLR multiplication. This section targets construction of multiple link tensors in parallel on GPUs. Naivly, one would need 𝒪⁡(L3)\mathcal{O}(L^{3}) HODLR multiplications to form all link tensors. However, since HOLDR multipication is associative, one can reduce the cost to O⁡(L2​log⁡L)O(L^{2}\log L) using a parallel prefix (Blelloch) scan [3].

Fix an endpoint b∈{1,…,L}b\in\{1,\dots,L\} and consider the reversed list (B(b),B(b−1),…,B(1))\bigl(B^{(b)},B^{(b-1)},\dots,B^{(1)}\bigr). A parallel prefix-scan over this list yields all prefix products

Pt(b)\displaystyle P^{(b)}_{t} :=B(b)⊙B(b−1)⊙⋯⊙B(b−t+1),t=1,…,b.\displaystyle:=B^{(b)}\odot B^{(b-1)}\odot\cdots\odot B^{(b-t+1)},\qquad t=1,\dots,b. (107)

These prefixes correspond exactly to consecutive products ending at bb via the index map

Xa,b\displaystyle X_{a,b} =Pb−a+1(b).\displaystyle=P^{(b)}_{\,b-a+1}. (108)

Thus, one scan computes the entire family {Xa,b}a=1b\{X_{a,b}\}_{a=1}^{b}. Running the same scan independently for different endpoints is precisely “parallel scans starting at different nodes” of the layer chain.

To construct all link tensors, for each target layer ℓ\ell we run a scan with endpoint b=ℓ−1b=\ell-1 to obtain all segments {Xm+1,ℓ−1}m=0ℓ−1\{X_{m+1,\ell-1}\}_{m=0}^{\ell-1} using Eq. (108). For each mm, we then form G(ℓ)​Xm+1,ℓ−1G^{(\ell)}X_{m+1,\ell-1} (HODLR multiply+recompress) and extract all local blocks ℒj(ℓ,m)\mathcal{L}^{(\ell,m)}_{j} using Eq. (106); all patch indices jj are independent and hence parallel.

H.5 Cost

Let one HODLR multiply+recompress cost

Tmm​(N,r)\displaystyle T_{\mathrm{mm}}(N,r) =Θ⁡(N​r2​log⁡(N/n0)).\displaystyle=\Theta\!\bigl(Nr^{2}\log(N/n_{0})\bigr). (109)

A scan of length bb uses Θ⁡(b)\Theta(b) HODLR multiplications (linear work) and has Θ⁡(log⁡b)\Theta(\log b) scan stages (logarithmic depth) [3]. Summing the work over endpoints b=1,…,Lb=1,\dots,L gives Θ⁡(L2)\Theta(L^{2}) HODLR multiplications, hence

Twork\displaystyle T_{\mathrm{work}} =Θ⁡(L2)​Tmm​(N,r)=Θ⁡(L2​N​r2​log⁡(N/n0)).\displaystyle=\Theta(L^{2})\,T_{\mathrm{mm}}(N,r)=\Theta\!\bigl(L^{2}Nr^{2}\log(N/n_{0})\bigr). (110)

Running all endpoint scans in parallel yields overall depth

Tdepth\displaystyle T_{\mathrm{depth}} =Θ⁡(log⁡L)​Tmm​(N,r).\displaystyle=\Theta(\log L)\,T_{\mathrm{mm}}(N,r). (111)

Forming B(ℓ)B^{(\ell)} in Eq. (103) by diagonal scaling is lower order than Eq. (110), and patch-block extraction in Eq. (106) is embarrassingly parallel over (ℓ,m,j)(\ell,m,j).

This scan-based construction therefore computes all cached link tensors with Θ⁡(log⁡L)\Theta(\log L) depth and log-linear HODLR costs in the system size NN. This shows link tensors for ABACUS can be efficiently constructed independent of network depth.

Appendix I DysonNet in two dimensions

We briefly extend the DysonNet block to a 2D lattice with N=Lx​LyN=L_{x}L_{y} sites. We index lattice sites by j=(jx,jy)j=(j_{x},j_{y}) and write translation-invariant kernels as functions of the displacement j−kj-k. The DysonNet block remains

Φ⁡(𝝈)​h=D⁡(𝝈)​G​h,\Phi(\bm{\sigma})\,h\;=\;D(\bm{\sigma})\,G\,h, (112)

with the same residual stacking and mean-pooling readout PMP_{M} as in the main text.

The 2D token mixer GG is a translationally invariant convolution operator (Toeplitz/circulant under periodic boundaries),

(G​h)j,c=∑rGj−r,c​hr,c,(Gh)_{j,c}\;=\;\sum_{r}G_{j-r,c}\,h_{r,c}, (113)

which is implemented with 2D FFTs channel-wise.

G​h=ℱ2−1​(ℱ2​(G)⊙ℱ2​(h)),Gh\;=\;\mathcal{F}_{2}^{-1}\!\big(\mathcal{F}_{2}(G)\odot\mathcal{F}_{2}(h)\big), (114)

where ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} denotes the discrete 2D Fourier transform over the Lx×LyL_{x}\times L_{y} grid and ⊙\odot is pointwise multiplication.

The local nonlinearity D⁡(𝝈)D(\bm{\sigma}) acts position-wise on each embedding vector, but may depend on a bounded patch around jj. Concretely, for a fixed patch radius ww define the square patch

Sj:={k:‖k−j‖∞≤w},W:=|Sj|=(2​w+1)2,S_{j}\;:=\;\{\,k:\ \|k-j\|_{\infty}\leq w\,\},\qquad W:=|S_{j}|=(2w+1)^{2}, (115)

and parameterize the local vertex as

(D⁡(𝝈)​h)j=D⁡(𝝈|Sj)​hj,(D(\bm{\sigma})h)_{j}\;=\;D\!\big(\bm{\sigma}|_{S_{j}}\big)\,h_{j}, (116)

i.e. D⁡(⋅)D(\cdot) “attends” to the WW tokens in the patch (via a small CNN/MLP over the patch) and outputs a d×dd\times d matrix multiplying the center token hjh_{j}.

For a single spin flip at position jj relative to a reference configuration 𝝈0\bm{\sigma}_{0}, we decompose each layer’s vertex as

D(l)​(𝝈)=D0(l)+Δ​D(l),D0(l):=D(l)​(𝝈0),D^{(l)}(\bm{\sigma})\;=\;D^{(l)}_{0}+\Delta D^{(l)},\qquad D^{(l)}_{0}:=D^{(l)}(\bm{\sigma}_{0}), (117)

where Δ​D(l)\Delta D^{(l)} is nonzero only on a bounded region: in 2D it is supported on (a small union of) patches around the flip, rather than on an interval. Let PS,jP_{S,j} denote the projector that restricts activations to the patch SjS_{j} (so PS,j​h∈ℝW×dP_{S,j}h\in\mathbb{R}^{W\times d}). Then the link tensors are defined exactly as before, with PS,jP_{S,j} now projecting onto a patch.

T(l)\displaystyle T^{(l)}\; =PM​Gf​(∑M=lL∏n=l+1MD0(n)​G(n))​PS,j⊤,\displaystyle=\;P_{M}\,G^{f}\!\left(\sum_{M=l}^{L}\prod_{n=l+1}^{M}D^{(n)}_{0}G^{(n)}\right)P_{S,j}^{\top}, (118)
L(l,m)\displaystyle L^{(l,m)}\; =PS,j​G(l)​(∏n=m+1l−1D0(n)​G(n))​PS,j⊤,1≤m≤l−2.\displaystyle=\;P_{S,j}\,G^{(l)}\!\left(\prod_{n=m+1}^{l-1}D^{(n)}_{0}G^{(n)}\right)P_{S,j}^{\top},\quad 1\leq m\leq l-2. (119)

Defining patch-restricted activations h~(l)=PS,j​h(l)∈ℝW×d\tilde{h}^{(l)}=P_{S,j}h^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{W\times d}, h~0(l)=PS,j​h0(l)\tilde{h}^{(l)}_{0}=P_{S,j}h^{(l)}_{0}, and G~(l):=PS,j​G(l)​PS,j⊤\tilde{G}^{(l)}:=P_{S,j}G^{(l)}P_{S,j}^{\top}, the DysonNet/ABACUS recurrence is unchanged except for interpreting the restriction as a patch.

h~(l)\displaystyle\tilde{h}^{(l)} =Δ​D(l)​(h~0(l)+G~(l)​h~(l−1)+∑m=1l−2L(l,m)​h~(m)),\displaystyle=\Delta D^{(l)}\left(\tilde{h}^{(l)}_{0}+\tilde{G}^{(l)}\tilde{h}^{(l-1)}+\sum_{m=1}^{l-2}L^{(l,m)}\tilde{h}^{(m)}\right), (120)
𝛀\displaystyle\qquad\bm{\Omega} =A⁡(PM​h~(L)+∑l=1LT(l)​h~(l)).\displaystyle=A\!\left(P_{M}\tilde{h}^{(L)}+\sum_{l=1}^{L}T^{(l)}\tilde{h}^{(l)}\right). (121)

Here G~(l)​h~(l−1)\tilde{G}^{(l)}\tilde{h}^{(l-1)} denotes propagating a patch-supported input through the convolution and then restricting back to the patch; operationally this is a contraction of the local (W×W)(W\times W) block of the Toeplitz operator (or an equivalent SSM restriction), exactly as in 1D.

Complexity statements carry over verbatim upon replacing the slice width W=2​w+1W=2w+1 by the patch size W=(2​w+1)2W=(2w+1)^{2}. Given precomputed links, the local-update runtime remains independent of NN and scales as O⁡(L2​W2​d2)O(L^{2}W^{2}d^{2}), Importantly, the link tensors depend on the number of tokens in the restricted region (WW), not on whether that region is a 1D interval or a 2D area. For DysonNet, link construction remains log-linear in NN because all required background propagations reduce to 2D convolutions, which are computed with 2D FFTs (and multi-layer links can be handled by the same low-rank probing strategy, with each probe dominated by O⁡(N​log⁡N)O(N\log N) FFT-based matvecs for fixed W,dW,d.

Appendix J Details on the implementation of the DysonNet block

Here we provide additional details on the implementation of S4 and the CNN.

Here we summarize the S4 parameterization from Ref. [24] in notation consistent with the main-text definitions in Eqs. (16) and (17). We start from the continuous-time state equation

∂x𝒚⁡(x)=A¯​𝒚​(x)+B¯​𝒉​(x).\displaystyle\partial_{x}\bm{y}(x)=\bar{A}\,\bm{y}(x)+\bar{B}\,\bm{h}(x). (122)

We discretize it with the bilinear transform

A\displaystyle A =(I−Δ2​A¯)−1​(I+Δ2​A¯),\displaystyle=\Bigl(I-\frac{\Delta}{2}\bar{A}\Bigr)^{-1}\Bigl(I+\frac{\Delta}{2}\bar{A}\Bigr), (123)
B\displaystyle B =(I−Δ2​A¯)−1​Δ​B¯.\displaystyle=\Bigl(I-\frac{\Delta}{2}\bar{A}\Bigr)^{-1}\Delta\bar{B}. (124)

where Δ\Delta is the step size. For zk=ei​2​π​k/Nz_{k}=e^{i2\pi k/N}, Eq. (17) becomes

Gc​(zk)\displaystyle G_{c}(z_{k}) =Cc​(I−zk​Ac)−1​Bc\displaystyle=C_{c}\,(I-z_{k}A_{c})^{-1}B_{c} (125)
=Cc​c​(zk)​(g⁡(zk)​I−Δ​A¯c)−1​B¯c.\displaystyle=C_{c}\,c(z_{k})\,\bigl(g(z_{k})I-\Delta\bar{A}_{c}\bigr)^{-1}\bar{B}_{c}. (126)

with

c⁡(z)=2​Δ1+z,g⁡(z)=2​(1−z)1+z.\displaystyle c(z)=\frac{2\Delta}{1+z},\qquad g(z)=\frac{2(1-z)}{1+z}. (127)

For diagonal A¯c=Λc\bar{A}_{c}=\Lambda_{c}, define the scalar Cauchy-kernel contraction

G^0,c​(z,u,v)=∑i=1svi​uig⁡(z)−Δ​Λc,i.\displaystyle\widehat{G}_{0,c}(z;u,v)=\sum_{i=1}^{s}\frac{v_{i}u_{i}}{g(z)-\Delta\Lambda_{c,i}}. (128)

For the S4 parameterization A¯c=Λc+𝒑c​𝒒c⊤\bar{A}_{c}=\Lambda_{c}+\bm{p}_{c}\bm{q}_{c}^{\top} (matching the main text), Woodbury gives [24]

Gc​(z)=c⁡(z)​(G^0,c​(z,B¯c,Cc)CLOSEOPEN−G^0,c​(z,𝒑c,Cc)​[1+G^0,c​(z,𝒑c,𝒒c∗)]−1​G^0,c​(z,B¯c,𝒒c∗)).\displaystyle\begin{split}G_{c}(z)&=c(z)\Big(\widehat{G}_{0,c}(z;\bar{B}_{c},C_{c})\\ &\quad-\widehat{G}_{0,c}(z;\bm{p}_{c},C_{c})\,[1+\widehat{G}_{0,c}(z;\bm{p}_{c},\bm{q}_{c}^{*})]^{-1}\widehat{G}_{0,c}(z;\bar{B}_{c},\bm{q}_{c}^{*})\Big).\end{split} (129)

This is the Green’s function practically implemented in our network.

For parameterizing the local vertex D⁡(𝝈)D(\bm{\sigma}) we use a short-ranged CNN kernel, as this enforces a finite receptive field Dj​(𝝈)=Dj​(σj−w,…,σj+w)D_{j}(\bm{\sigma})=D_{j}(\sigma_{j-w},\dots,\sigma_{j+w}). In our model we create a second data stream ϕ(l)\bm{\phi}^{(l)} (see Fig. 1c) with vectors ϕj(l)∈ℝd\bm{\phi}_{j}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} for sites j=1,…,Nj=1,\dots,N. We compute ϕ(1)=Eϕ​𝝈\bm{\phi}^{(1)}=E_{\phi}\bm{\sigma} with embedding matrix Eϕ∈ℝd×1E_{\phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times 1}. Each layer applies (i) a site-wise dense map, (ii) a short-range depth-wise convolution, and (iii) an elementwise nonlinearity gg (we use SiLU\mathrm{SiLU}).

ϕ~j(l)\displaystyle\bm{\tilde{\phi}}_{j}^{(l)} =WD(l)​ϕj(l)+𝒘(l),\displaystyle=W_{D}^{(l)}\bm{\phi}_{j}^{(l)}+\bm{w}^{(l)}, (130)
ϕj(l+1)\displaystyle\bm{\phi}_{j}^{(l+1)} =g⁡(∑r=−wwKr(l)⊙ϕ~j+r(l)+𝒌(l)).\displaystyle=g\!\bigg(\sum_{r=-w}^{w}K_{r}^{(l)}\odot\bm{\tilde{\phi}}_{j+r}^{(l)}+\bm{k}^{(l)}\bigg). (131)

Here, WD(l)∈ℝd×dW_{D}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} and 𝒘(l)∈ℝd\bm{w}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} are the site-wise (dense) weight matrix and bias at layer ll. The convolution has half-width ww with offsets r∈[−w,w]r\in[-w,w]; indices j+rj+r are taken modulo NN (circular padding). Kr(l)∈ℝdK_{r}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the kernel at offset rr and 𝒌(l)∈ℝd\bm{k}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} its bias. The nonlinearity is applied element-wise and chosen as SiLU\mathrm{SiLU}: g⁡(x)=SiLU⁡(x)=x/(1+e−x)g(x)=\mathrm{SiLU}(x)=x/(1+e^{-x}).

To match Eq. (19), we define

χ⁡(ϕj(l−1))\displaystyle\chi(\bm{\phi}^{(l-1)}_{j}) =g⁡(AD(l)​ϕj(l−1)+𝒃(l)),\displaystyle=g\!\big(A_{D}^{(l)}\bm{\phi}^{(l-1)}_{j}+\bm{b}^{(l)}\big), (132)
Dj​(𝝈)\displaystyle D_{j}(\bm{\sigma}) =U(l)​diag​(χ⁡(ϕj(l−1)))​V(l).\displaystyle=U^{(l)}\,\mathrm{diag}\!\big(\chi(\bm{\phi}^{(l-1)}_{j})\big)\,V^{(l)}. (133)

Here AD(l)∈ℝd×dA_{D}^{(l)}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} and 𝒃(l)∈ℝd\bm{b}^{(l)}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d} are trainable dense weights, and gg is an elementwise nonlinearity (we use SiLU\mathrm{SiLU}). The vector χ⁡(ϕj(l−1))∈ℝd\chi(\bm{\phi}^{(l-1)}_{j})\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d} parametrizes the configuration-dependent spectrum, while U(l),V(l)∈ℝd×dU^{(l)},V^{(l)}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} are layer-specific, configuration-independent bases (fixed left/right “eigenvectors”). Thus Dj​(𝝈)∈ℝd×dD_{j}(\bm{\sigma})\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} has fixed eigenvectors but spin-configuration–dependent eigenvalues through ϕj(l−1)\bm{\phi}^{(l-1)}_{j}. As in the main text, we also inject the ϕ(l)\bm{\phi}^{(l)} stream additively into the mixer stream before applying the SSM. In this work we take the parameters to be real. We note as this is inside the network this does not limit expressivity to real valued wavefunctions, as a complex vector can be embedded in a real-valued vector space. The final layer determines the sign structure of the network 11 1 If a symmetric parameterization is desired, one may set V(l)=U(l)⊤V^{(l)}\!=\!U^{(l)\top}..

Appendix K Small system validation TFIM

We evaluate the neural quantum state (NQS) for the long-ranged transverse-field Ising model at N=20N=20 on a 2D parameter grid—vertical axis J∈[−5,5]J\in[-5,5], horizontal axis α∈[0,6]\alpha\in[0,6]; see Fig. 6. At each grid point we report the overlap error (infidelity) with the exact ground state. The fidelity is F=|⟨Ψ0|ΨNQS⟩|2F=|\langle\Psi_{0}|\Psi_{\mathrm{NQS}}\rangle|^{2}; in the presence of a (near-)degenerate ground-state manifold we compute the overlap with the ground-state subspace, F=∑j|⟨Ψ0,j|ΨNQS⟩|2F=\sum_{j}|\langle\Psi_{0,j}|\Psi_{\mathrm{NQS}}\rangle|^{2}, treating states as degenerate when their energy splitting is <10−6<10^{-6}. The right panel of Fig. 6 shows the ground-state energy error, Δ​E=|E0−ENQS|\Delta E=|E_{0}-E_{\mathrm{NQS}}|. For each grid point we perform three independent training runs and report the median; no training instabilities were observed.

Across the grid, the median infidelity is 2.99×10−42.99\times 10^{-4}: most points sit at ≲10−3\lesssim 10^{-3}, with a few localized pockets reaching ∼10−2\sim 10^{-2} near short-ranged (large-α\alpha) critical regions where optimization is harder—still small in absolute terms. Ground-state energies are uniformly accurate: typical Δ​E\Delta E is 22–5×10−45\times 10^{-4}, spanning 8.83×10−58.83\times 10^{-5} to 9.54×10−49.54\times 10^{-4}. Overall, energies are robust across the phase diagram, while fidelity remains tight almost everywhere and softens only mildly near criticality.

Appendix L Critical exponents and finite-size scaling

To test whether DysonNet captures not only ground-state energies but also the long-distance structure of critical wavefunctions, we perform a finite-size-scaling analysis of the long-range TFIM at representative interaction exponents spanning the distinct universality regimes. Specifically, we compute the squared magnetization ⟨m2⟩\langle m^{2}\rangle for a range of system sizes and couplings near criticality and collapse the data using the scaling form

N2​β/ν​⟨m2⟩=f⁡((J−Jc)​N1/ν),\displaystyle N^{2\beta/\nu}\langle m^{2}\rangle=f\!\left((J-J_{c})N^{1/\nu}\right), (134)

with JcJ_{c}, ν\nu, and β\beta treated as fit parameters. The collapse is obtained using the PyFSSA package [71], and the quoted uncertainties are estimated conservatively as the maximum of two procedures: a jackknife analysis in which one system size is omitted at a time, and a bootstrap resampling analysis over the full dataset.

The resulting collapses, shown in Fig. 7, are of high quality across all three representative values of α\alpha, demonstrating that DysonNet reproduces the universal critical behavior of the model rather than merely fitting local observables or variational energies. The extracted critical exponents listed in Table 2 agree closely with stochastic-series-expansion benchmarks and known theoretical predictions. Together, these results show that the architecture remains accurate even at criticality and that access to larger system sizes substantially improves the reliability of exponent extraction.

Appendix M Small system validation J1J_{1}–J2J_{2}

The antiferromagnetic J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model is the spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg chain with competing nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor exchange,

H=J1​∑i=1N𝐒^i⋅𝐒^i+1+J2​∑i=1N𝐒^i⋅𝐒^i+2,H=J_{1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i+1}+J_{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i+2}, (135)

with periodic boundary conditions. For 0<J2/J1≲0.240<J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 0.24 the ground state remains critical and is well described by a Luttinger liquid with algebraically decaying spin correlations, while increasing J2J_{2} introduces frustration that reshapes short- and intermediate-range correlations [53, 18, 84]. At J2/J1≃0.24J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 0.24 the chain undergoes a Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition into a gapped, spontaneously dimerized phase, which continuously connects to the Majumdar–Ghosh point at J2/J1=1/2J_{2}/J_{1}=1/2 where the ground state is exactly a product of singlet dimers (up to a twofold translation degeneracy) [53, 47]. This combination of (i) a well-established phase diagram containing both critical and gapped regimes, (ii) strong frustration and entanglement that stress variational expressivity, and (iii) exact-diagonalization access at small NN makes the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} chain a standard, stringent benchmark for many-body wavefunction ansätze [7, 44, 79].

Building on this standard benchmark, we evaluate the DysonNet architecture on the antiferromagnetic J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} chain with N=20N=20 sites across the frustration range 0≤J2/J1≤0.50\leq J_{2}/J_{1}\leq 0.5 (Fig. 8). DysonNet maintains high accuracy throughout, with the relative ground-state energy error ε\varepsilon remaining below 4×10−44\times 10^{-4} for all couplings. The error reaches a minimum of 2.17×10−52.17\times 10^{-5} at J2/J1≈0.08J_{2}/J_{1}\approx 0.08 and then increases smoothly with frustration, attaining a maximum of 3.71×10−43.71\times 10^{-4} near the strongly frustrated regime. Importantly, we observe no sharp loss of precision in the vicinity of the quantum critical point at J2/J1≈0.24J_{2}/J_{1}\approx 0.24 [53, 18], suggesting that DysonNet captures the ground-state correlations consistently across the transition. The variational V-score mirrors this trend, ranging from 1.91×10−41.91\times 10^{-4} to 2.44×10−32.44\times 10^{-3}.

Appendix N Network parameters

Unless otherwise stated, optimization uses standard SR and TF32 precision on NVIDIA GPUs. Sweep counts are scaled linearly with system size NN in all phases, including area-law regimes. Chains are randomly initialized, the burn-in length is five sweeps, and global spin inversion is attempted after every ⌈N/(2​w+1)⌉\left\lceil N/(2w+1)\right\rceil proposals. For the RBM baseline we use hidden-unit density αRBM=10\alpha_{\mathrm{RBM}}=10 (Nh=10​NvN_{h}=10N_{v}), which is distinct from the Hamiltonian decay exponent α\alpha. Most training runs use NVIDIA Tesla P100, T4, and L4 GPUs; the largest runs on criticality (N>600N>600) are executed on a single NVIDIA A40. We note or N<500N<500 DysonNet can be trained in google collab or Kaggle notebooks, meaning DysonNet makes large system sizes generally accessible without the need for high-end compute clusters. For finite-size scaling we warm-start larger systems from converged smaller systems. Critical exponents are extracted with PyFSSA [71]. Uncertainties for the critical exponents are computed by taking the maximum over the bootstrapping and jacknife approach.
